title: A Korean Odyssey
hookNote: Episode 5, once the contract between them is actually binding.
endingText: The bargain at the centre has a price and the show makes it pay, then softens the final minutes.
verdict: The Hong sisters rewriting Journey to the West as a contract between a demon and the woman who can see ghosts, made under a production so troubled it had to apologise on air. Lee Seung Gi and Cha Seung Won are having an enormous amount of fun and the mythology is the most interesting thing the pair have written. It takes five episodes to become watchable and the effects work is rough in places you will notice. The back half is stronger than the front, which is the reverse of the usual problem here.

title: A Shop for Killers
hookNote: Episode 1. The uncle is dead, the house is under attack, and the flashback structure starts working straight away.
endingText: The siege resolves and the family question is answered, with one thread left standing for a second season.
verdict: Eight episodes of a woman defending a house full of weapons she was trained to use without knowing she was being trained. The structure is the trick: a present-day siege cut against a childhood of quiet, deniable preparation, so every flashback pays off as ammunition. Kim Hye Jun carries it and Lee Dong Wook is used sparingly and well. Some of the assassins are cartoons and the drone effects are rough. Still the tightest Korean action series since Bloodhounds, and a great deal smarter.

title: Agent Kim Reactivated
hookNote: Episode 1. A retired operative, a taken daughter, and no interest in explaining physics. The pace only breaks at episodes 8 and 9.
endingText: Satisfying and complete after a real wobble: two late episodes lose the thread before the finale pulls everything back into place.
verdict: The biggest broadcast hit of 2026 and it earns the numbers. So Ji Sub plays a savings bank manager who used to be a very effective spy, his daughter is taken, and the show gives him two middle aged friends with one outfit each and the same impossible skill set. It is Taken with a Korean webtoon logic, and the trio is what makes it more than that: three men past their prime, deeply unserious about themselves and lethal anyway. Logic left in the first ten minutes and never came back. Episodes 8 and 9 sag badly. Watch it for the action and the friendship, and do not think about the school violence subplot too hard.

title: Alchemy of Souls
hookNote: Episode 3, once the training arc starts and the ensemble locks in.
endingText: Part 1 stops on a hard cliff that requires Part 2. Watched back to back it resolves; watched alone it will irritate you.
verdict: The best looking fantasy Korea has made and the most frustrating structure. Part one is twenty episodes of body-swap romance running on a training arc, and for about twelve of them it is superb: funny, gorgeous, built on a lead pair with real chemistry. Then it repeats itself, stretches, and stops on a cliff that requires part two, which recasts the female lead and changes the tone completely. Do not start this unless you intend to watch both parts. It rewatches poorly for a show this loved, which tells you how much of the pleasure is plot.

title: Alchemy of Souls Part 2: Light and Shadow
hookNote: Episode 1, which is as good as it gets. This is the one entry in the catalog with no hook, because the per-episode ratings open at their highest and fall for the rest of the run.
endingText: It closes the whole story, both leads included, and needs no third part. The resolution is crammed into the final hour, so it lands as relief rather than payoff.
verdict: Watch it for closure, not for pleasure. Part 1 ended on a cliff and this is the only place the story finishes, so if you need the ending you have no choice, and it does deliver a conclusive happy one. Everything else is worse: the recast lead plays a different character rather than the same one, the amnesia plot eats roughly eight of the ten hours, and the swordswoman who ran Part 1 spends most of this captive. Ten episodes should have fixed Part 1's bloat, and instead the plot stands still until the last two hours and then rushes. The production and the action are a step up, which was never the problem.

title: Another Miss Oh
hookNote: Episode 3, once both Oh Hae Youngs are inside the same story.
endingText: The premonition thread resolves kindly and the couple lands, after a stretch where the show threatens otherwise.
verdict: Park Hae Young writing a romcom two years before she wrote My Mister, and the dialogue gives it away: two people talking past each other for hours with a precision nothing else in this bracket has. Seo Hyun Jin is extraordinary, playing humiliation as comedy without once asking to be pitied. The premonition device is a mistake, dragging a life-or-death plot into a show that was better as an argument about being second choice, and the last third suffers for it. Rewatch scores are the lowest of any romance here at under five out of ten, which is what happens when the pleasure is all in the surprise.

title: At a Distance, Spring Is Green
query: At a Distance Spring is Green
hookNote: Episode 2, once the three of them are stuck working together and the masks start slipping.
endingText: Nothing is cured. Two damaged people say out loud that they need help, and the show calls that progress.
verdict: A campus drama that hides a depression story inside a friendship story, and the friendship is the better half. Park Ji Hoon and Bae In Hyuk carry it with a bromance that earns more investment than the romantic subplot, which arrives late and leaves early. Twelve episodes is the right length: it says what it has to say about isolation and performative happiness without padding. The romance never catches up to the male friendships, and that gap is the only real flaw.

title: Because This Is My First Life
query: Because This Is My First Life
hookNote: Episode 2, once the housemate arrangement starts.
endingText: Both leads choose each other on purpose rather than by accident. Side couples resolve cleanly.
verdict: The contract marriage premise with the silliness taken out. A house-poor man and a homeless writer sign what is really a lease, and the drama turns it into an argument about whether marriage is a romance or an economic arrangement. Jung So Min and Lee Min Ki play it quiet and adult, which is rare, and which is also why stretches of the middle feel airless. The two side couples carry more weight than the poster suggests, and episode fifteen manufactures a separation the story did not need. Still the smartest thing here about being thirty and broke.
aliases: Porque esta es mi primera vida

title: Beyond Evil
hookNote: Episode 3, the point at which you stop trusting both leads at once. The bigger shift is episode 9: the first eight ask whether he did it, the last eight answer a different question, and that is where opinion splits.
endingText: The truth comes out completely and costs both men something permanent. The final scene is quiet and fully earned.
verdict: Two policemen who each believe the other is a murderer, and neither of them is wrong about how far the other will go. It is the best acted thing in this catalog: Shin Ha Kyun and Yeo Jin Goo circle each other for sixteen hours and the ambiguity is maintained honestly instead of by withholding information. The plot does loop, and the middle stretch repeats its own reveals more than it should. It is heavy, and the small town setting keeps everything airless. Worth every minute if you want a mystery about complicity rather than a whodunnit.

title: Beyond the Bar
hookNote: Episode 2. The mentor and the rookie stop performing at each other and the case work takes over, and the ratings sit above nine for most of the run.
endingText: The cases close and the central relationship is deliberately left mid sentence, which is the one choice that splits an otherwise clean run.
verdict: A legal drama that earns its mentor-junior dynamic honestly and then refuses to resolve the personal relationship, which is either mature restraint or cowardice depending on your patience. The case work is solid, the courtroom scenes are among the better ones in recent memory, and the twelve episodes never pad. The deliberate ambiguity of the ending is the one choice that splits an otherwise clean run.
aliases: Esquire: Lawyers Dreaming of Becoming Lawyers

title: Bitter Sweet Hell
hookNote: Episode 1. The affair is discovered and the alliance with the mother in law forms fast.
endingText: The marriage question is settled and the two women come out of it holding the upper hand.
verdict: A psychological thriller wrapped in a black comedy about a marriage falling apart, and the mother-in-law alliance is the best thing in it. The gaslighting is played for tension rather than shock, and the show is smart enough to make both women competent rather than making one a victim. Twelve episodes on MBC, a 7.7 rating that reflects the niche rather than the quality, and a tone that most audiences will either love for its sharpness or bounce off for its meanness.

title: Blood Free
hookNote: Episode 4, once the corporate thriller shows what it is actually about.
endingText: The conspiracy closes on a deliberately open note that suits the ideas more than the plot.
verdict: A biotech thriller from the writer of Stranger, and the intelligence of the writing is the draw. Ju Ji Hoon and Han Hyo Joo play the conspiracy straight, the science fiction elements are used for ideas rather than spectacle, and the ten episodes never condescend. It is heavy on politics and light on action, which is exactly the show it set out to be. The ending is deliberately open, which suits the ideas and frustrates the plot.

title: Bloodhounds
hookNote: Episode 1. The boxing gym and the loan-shark hook are both done inside one episode.
endingText: The villain is beaten, the debt plot closes, and the two friends walk away together.
verdict: Eight episodes, two boxers, and the best hand-to-hand choreography Netflix has paid for in Korea. The plot is thin and the villain is a cartoon, and neither matters, because the friendship at the centre is warm and the fights are staged so you can read every exchange. Watch it for the two of them. This is the season to start with and the better of the two.

title: Bloodhounds Season 2
hookNote: Episode 3, once the new operation is properly on screen. The first two hours are spent re-introducing people you already know.
endingText: It does not close. The debt plot from season one stays closed, but the new antagonist is deliberately left standing and the final minutes are a setup for a third season.
verdict: Only worth it if the fights were why you watched. The choreography is better than season one and everything around it is worse: the plotting is slack, the new antagonist never earns his runtime, and the show keeps mistaking the hero crying for the hero having an interior life. Season one survived a thin plot because the friendship carried it, and this one separates the friendship for long stretches and has nothing to put in its place. Finished airing April 2026. Start it for the choreography, expect no ending.

title: Bloody Flower
hookNote: Episode 1 is the high point of the run by a clear margin. Everything after it is a slow decline in per-episode ratings.
endingText: Climactic and underwhelming at once, with one deliberate ambiguity left in place and a few details never explained.
verdict: An eight-episode thriller on Disney+ that peaks at episode one and declines from there. The premiere is genuinely unsettling, the human-experimentation premise is strong, and then the show stretches rather than sharpens, leaving several details unexplained and one ambiguity in place that feels like laziness rather than design. A 7.8 from under fifteen thousand ratings, and the small audience is telling.

title: Bon Appetit, Your Majesty
hookNote: Episode 3, once the cooking competition format kicks in. The ratings peak at episode 4 and never get back there.
endingText: The timeslip gets an answer and the pairing gets its scene. The palace plot is cleared away far faster than it was built.
verdict: A modern chef falls into Joseon and cooks for a tyrant, and for four episodes the food is genuinely worth the runtime. Lee Chae Min is the find here, playing the king as a spoiled connoisseur who is dangerous only when the food is bad. After that the show discovers it has twelve hours of eighty minutes to fill and no story to fill them with, so the dishes get more attention than the characters and the romance never leaves the kitchen. Yoona is fine and underserved. Watch it hungry, at speed, and do not expect the palace politics to mean anything.

title: Boyfriend on Demand
hookNote: Episode 1 is the entire concept and the show never escalates past it. If the subscription gag has not won you by the end of the first hour, stop there.
endingText: Happy, and exactly the one the premise telegraphs in its opening minutes.
verdict: A burnt out webtoon producer subscribes to a virtual boyfriend service and gets a rotating cast of cameos. The idea is timely and the show does nothing with it: no escalation, no cost, no argument about what she is actually buying, just a very expensive parade of outfits and famous faces. Ji Soo and Seo In Guk are pleasant and stranded. It is not offensively bad, which is worse, because a premise about outsourcing intimacy in 2026 should provoke something. Watch it on second screen or skip it and watch Dynamite Kiss, which fails at the same job with more charm.

title: Brewing Love
hookNote: Episode 3, once the brewery plot and the romance are pointed in the same direction.
endingText: The brewery survives and the couple ends together, with no late obstacle worth the name.
verdict: A village romcom about a special-forces veteran brewing beer in the countryside, and the first two episodes are so slow that the rest of the show has to recover from them. It does recover, eventually, and the leads have a warmth that carries the middle stretch. The tone is wildly inconsistent, swinging between sensitive character study and broad slapstick inside the same episode, and the beer-brewing plot never quite justifies its own existence. A pleasant watch that cannot decide what kind of show it wants to be.

title: Buried Hearts
hookNote: Episode 7, and it genuinely improves from there: the ratings climb through the back half and the last two hours are the best of the run.
endingText: Open ended and abrupt, and it withholds the one answer the sixteen hours were built around.
verdict: A political crime drama that asks you to wait seven episodes for the hook and then delivers genuinely improving back-half drama, only to pull the rug with an abrupt, open ending that withholds the one answer the sixteen hours were built around. Park Hyung Sik deserved better, and so did everyone who watched. The production is slick, the corruption mechanics are interesting, and the ending makes all of it feel pointless.

title: Business Proposal
hookNote: Episode 1. It commits to the bit in the first ten minutes, and that is the appeal.
endingText: Zero jeopardy. Both couples land exactly where the pilot promised, with a wedding-adjacent epilogue.
verdict: Twelve hours of cliches executed with total conviction, and the conviction is why it works. The point is speed and the second couple: the friend and the heiress are better written than the leads and get most of the good lines. There is no depth here, the office plot is cardboard, and it never once pretends otherwise. Best taken two episodes at a time in a bad week. If you want a romance that argues with you, this is the wrong one.

title: Call It Love
hookNote: Episode 4, once the revenge plan stops being a plan and becomes a habit of seeing each other.
endingText: The revenge is abandoned rather than completed, and the two of them end up somewhere quiet and honest.
verdict: A revenge melodrama where the revenge plan dissolves into a habit of showing up for each other, and the dissolving is the whole point. It is glacially slow, deliberately so, and the payoff is quiet rather than dramatic: two exhausted people deciding they can stop performing. Lee Sung Kyung plays the prickliest female lead of the year and makes it feel protective rather than hostile. Not for anyone who needs things to happen at pace, but honest about grief in a way romances almost never are.

title: Can This Love Be Translated?
hookNote: Episode 1. The meet cute in Kamakura is the whole pitch and it is the best hour in the run, so if it does not land nothing later will.
endingText: The couple resolves and the career mess around them gets half tidied. The final two hours are busier and less certain than the ten in front of them.
verdict: The premise is the best thing in Korean romance this year: an interpreter whose job is to be invisible is assigned to a star whose public voice he has been quietly rewriting, so every press conference is a live test of what he is willing to say for her. Kim Seon Ho is very good at the stillness this needs and Go Youn Jung is better, because the private version of her character is genuinely unpleasant and she never softens it to be likeable. Then the Hong sisters do what the Hong sisters do and pile on a second and third idea, and by the back half it is three shows fighting for twelve hours. Worth it for the first six episodes and the acting. Do not expect the ending to be as clever as the setup.

title: Captivating the King
hookNote: Episode 8, where the spying finally has consequences. Getting there takes eight slow hours.
endingText: The throne plot resolves and the romance pays for it. Nobody ends where they hoped to.
verdict: A sageuk romance that takes eight episodes to reach its hook and never fully recovers from the wait. Jo Jung Suk is commanding as the king and the palace politics have genuine teeth, but the romance never generates the chemistry the title promises, and Shin Se Kyung's role is underwritten relative to the screen time it occupies. The Go game conceit is the most interesting structural idea and it is abandoned too early. An 8.0 from nineteen thousand ratings, and the gap between the political thriller and the love story is the entire problem.

title: Castaway Diva
hookNote: Episode 2, once she is off the island and actually singing.
endingText: The abuse plot is confronted directly rather than dodged, and she gets the career. Everyone who needed rescuing is rescued.
verdict: Park Eun Bin is the reason to watch and the island premise is the reason to start. The first two episodes are genuinely affecting: the backstory is earned, the singing is real, and the rescue lands. It fumbles the transition to modern Seoul badly, the abuse subplot is handled with more courage than finesse, and several characters exist to deliver exposition rather than to live. Still worth the twelve hours for the performance and the music, but the screenplay is not in the same league as the lead.

title: Cheese in the Trap
hookNote: Episode 1. The dynamic between them is unsettling from the first scene.
endingText: It ends abruptly with the central relationship unresolved, which was a production problem rather than a choice.
verdict: The best-observed campus drama here and the worst-managed production. Kim Go Eun and Park Hae Jin are excellent, and the first ten episodes are a quietly frightening study of a man who manages people instead of liking them. Then screen time gets rearranged around the second lead, the central relationship goes missing from its own show, and the finale rates lowest of the run at 7.5 for good reason. Worth watching for what it does right up front, as long as you know it never finishes the thought.

title: Chicago Typewriter
hookNote: Episode 1. The typewriter and the debt arrive in the first hour.
endingText: The past is settled rather than rewritten, so the resolution costs something and the present-day thread lands softly.
verdict: A blocked novelist, a ghostwriter, and a typewriter that remembers 1930s Gyeongseong, and it is far better than that logline suggests. The colonial-era half is the real show, three friends in a resistance cell written with enough weight that the modern half becomes a story about owing something to the dead. Yoo Ah In and Go Kyung Pyo are superb, the ratings sit at 9.4 and above for the entire back half, and it never explains itself twice. The present-day publishing comedy is the weak strand and it is still funny.

title: Chicken Nugget
hookNote: Episode 1. A woman climbs into a machine and comes out as a chicken nugget. Either you are in or you are not.
endingText: It answers the nugget question and then goes one idea further, which is entirely in character.
verdict: Ten half hour episodes built on the stupidest premise in Korean television, played with a completely straight face. Ryu Seung Ryong is a father searching for his deep fried daughter, Ahn Jae Hong is the intern helping him, and the show keeps escalating into places no summary can prepare you for. The aggregate score is low because it looks like a one line joke and is actually a formal experiment. Funniest Korean drama of 2024, and not for everyone.

title: Chief Detective 1958
hookNote: Episode 1. The squad assembles fast and the case a week rhythm starts immediately.
endingText: The corruption case closes, the squad survives, and the framing story lands the final scene.
verdict: A period detective comedy set in 1958 Seoul with Lee Je Hoon playing the future legendary detective as a young hothead, and the result is ten episodes of pure entertainment. The squad assembles fast, the case-a-week rhythm works, and the period detail is played for charm rather than grit. It is lightweight by design, and the framing device connecting 1958 to 2023 is sweet rather than deep. Best watched without expectations of anything heavy.

title: Connection
hookNote: Episode 1. The forced addiction happens straight away and the countdown starts with it.
endingText: The conspiracy is exposed and the detective's own situation resolves at a price.
verdict: A narcotics thriller where the detective is forcibly addicted to the drug he is investigating, and the premise creates a physical urgency that most procedurals lack. Ji Sung carries fourteen episodes with a performance that makes the withdrawal feel real, and the supporting cast, particularly the journalist, is strong. The conspiracy is resolved cleanly and the personal cost is not waved away. A tight, well-acted crime drama that knows what it is and does not try to be anything else.

title: Crash Course in Romance
hookNote: Episode 3, once the side-dish shop and the cram school collide properly.
endingText: A thriller subplot lands harder than the genre promised, then family and couple both settle warmly.
verdict: A romcom that smuggles a surprisingly effective thriller into the middle of a cram school love story. Jeon Do Yeon and Jung Kyung Ho play the age gap romance as adults rather than blushing teenagers, which is the single best decision the show makes. The killer subplot hits harder than the genre promises and the comedy lands more often than it misses. Sixteen episodes is two too many, the way it always is, but the ensemble and the Gangnam education satire keep it alive when the romance coasts.

title: Crash Landing on You
hookNote: Episode 2, the moment the village women turn up at his door. The soldiers and the neighbours are the show.
endingText: The border does not conveniently vanish, but the story finds a workaround that holds. Everyone you liked gets a landing.
verdict: The most watched Korean drama outside Korea, and the first half earns the number. The village is the actual draw: the soldier's neighbours and his squad are funnier and warmer than the romance they surround, and the comedy is far better than the premise suggests. It sags once the story moves south and has to keep inventing reasons for two people to be in the same country, and the assassin subplot is dead weight. Hyun Bin and Son Ye Jin are worth the sag. Watch it for the North Korean village and treat the last four episodes as the price of the first twelve.

title: Daily Dose of Sunshine
hookNote: Episode 1, which sets the format: one patient, one nurse, one small mercy, repeated for twelve hours.
endingText: The nurse comes out the other side of her own illness and the show refuses to call it a cure.
verdict: A nurse moves to the psychiatric ward and the show hands each episode to a different patient, with animation standing in for what illness feels like from the inside. Park Bo Young is exact and the ward staff are written like colleagues rather than saints. It looks like comfort viewing and it is not: the pastel packaging sits on top of depression, self harm and burnout, and a 5.2 rewatch score against an 8.8 aggregate is what that mismatch does to people. Kind, careful, much heavier than the title.
aliases: Un Raggio di Sole al Giorno
Morning Comes to the Mental Ward
Morning Comes to Psychiatric Wards Too

title: Dear Hongrang
hookNote: Episode 1. A missing heir returns and nobody in the house believes he is who he says, and the ratings hold above nine the whole way.
endingText: The identity question is answered and the cost is paid in full. The political half of the plot gets tidied away in a hurry.
verdict: A Joseon mystery built on a missing heir who returns with no memory, and for the first half the show is gripping: gorgeous production, genuine suspense, and a lead pair with intense chemistry. The second half collapses. The political plot is rushed, the mystery's answer is less interesting than the question, and the bittersweet ending lands heavy. A show that deserved a better back half than it got.

title: Dear My Friends
hookNote: Episode 3, once the friend group's shared history stops being backstory.
endingText: Noh Hee-kyung refuses a tidy bow. Losses are absorbed and the group carries on, louder than before.
verdict: The best written drama almost nobody has watched: 4,600 ratings against Goblin's hundred thousand, and it is the better show. Noh Hee Kyung hands it to actresses in their seventies and lets them be funny, petty, terrified and unfinished, which Korean television does not do with older women. The young translator narrating it is the weakest thing in it, a protagonist bolted on for an audience that did not need her. It is heavier than the warm poster implies and the last two hours are brutal. Watch it for the four or five performances you will not see anywhere else.

title: Death's Game
hookNote: Episode 1. The premise is fully explained inside twenty minutes and the first body swap happens before the hour is up.
endingText: The last life closes the loop and the show insists on a moral lesson that not everybody will accept.
verdict: A man who has failed at everything takes his own life and is sentenced to die twelve more times in twelve borrowed bodies. The cast is absurd, the structure is propulsive, and Seo In Guk holds twelve different performances together with real control. The problem is what it says: the framing turns suicide into a punishable failure of effort, and by the sixth life the show is arguing with the character rather than about anything. Eight fast hours with a message you may want to throw something at.

title: Descendants of the Sun
hookNote: Episode 1. The meet-cute and the deployment are both loaded inside the first hour.
endingText: It resolves warmly, but the final stretch takes back something it made you sit with, and the epilogue papers over the cost.
verdict: The show that sold Korean drama to a continent, and the first eight hours deserve it: Song Joong Ki and Song Hye Kyo carry dialogue built almost entirely out of flirting under fire. It is two shows stapled together, a military romance and a disaster procedural, and the second couple is better written than the first. The last two hours reach for a twist that undoes its own stakes, which is the one reason it does not sit higher. Come for the leads and the Urk scenery and accept that the plot is scaffolding.

title: Destined with You
hookNote: Episode 2, once the spell book is actually opened and the show commits to being a comedy about a curse.
endingText: The curse is lifted, the past life is settled, and the last hour is pure epilogue.
verdict: A civil servant inherits a wooden chest of spells and accidentally lands a love potion on the chaebol lawyer who has been cursed for six hundred years. It is a silly premise played with total conviction, and Jo Bo Ah and Rowoon have the chemistry to carry it: the written reviews average 8.5, which is high for a fantasy romcom. The horror side plot is undercooked and the middle four episodes stall while the show explains its own mythology twice. Come for the leads, not the lore.

title: Divorce Attorney Shin
hookNote: Episode 2, once the case-per-episode rhythm and the friend group both settle.
endingText: The long personal grudge is resolved in court and the friendships come out intact.
verdict: A divorce procedural with a warm centre and a case-of-the-week structure that works better than the overarching plot. Cho Seung Woo is steady and understated, and the supporting cast, especially the rival attorney, is stronger than the lead couple. It runs out of energy around episode ten and the final cases land softer than the opening ones. Pleasant, competent, and unlikely to be thought about a month later.

title: Doubt
hookNote: Episode 1. The profiler finds his own daughter inside his case before the first hour is out.
endingText: The case is solved and the family does not recover from the solving.
verdict: A criminal profiler discovers his own daughter inside his own case, and the ten episodes that follow are a slow, painful narrowing of that premise. Han Suk Kyu leads with the kind of restrained despair that makes silence feel loud, and the show is genuinely psychological rather than merely branded as one. It is not for everyone: the pace is deliberate, the answers come late, and the family does not recover from the solving. A good thriller that prioritises damage over closure.

title: D.P.
hookNote: Episode 1. Six episodes, and the first deserter case establishes the entire pattern.
endingText: One case ends badly enough to change both leads permanently. Season one stops on a deliberate refusal to resolve.
verdict: Six episodes, and the rare Korean drama that forced a real institution to answer for itself. Two military police catch deserters, and every case is a study of what the barracks did to the man before he ran. It is funny for about twenty minutes and then it is not funny at all, and the last two episodes are as good as television gets. There is no relief and no romance, and the final scene refuses to close on purpose. The best thing Netflix has commissioned in Korea.

title: D.P. Season 2
hookNote: Episode 3. The first two hours are spent assembling a conspiracy, and episode 3 is where the season remembers it is about two men and the institution above them.
endingText: It ends in a hearing, where one speech does most of the emotional work. The institution is left standing on purpose and the last minutes are built for a third season.
verdict: Season one put a boot on your chest for six hours. This one builds a conspiracy instead, with a villain at the top of the system, which makes the story bigger and much less frightening. It also thins as it goes: the third hour is the strongest and the last two are the weakest of either season, because a court case cannot do what a barracks did. Jung Hae In is still exceptional and the closing hearing has real force. Worth it if season one wrecked you and you want the argument finished rather than the wound reopened.

title: Dynamite Kiss
hookNote: Episode 1, which is the highest rated hour of the run. The decline is steady from episode 3 and steep across the last two.
endingText: Sweetened and predictable, after two final hours of obstacles the story never needed.
verdict: An office romcom that loads every cliche in the genre into the first episode and then has nowhere to go but down. The Jeju fling is fun, the reunion at the company is predictable, and the last two episodes manufacture obstacles the story never needed. The ratings decline is steady from episode three onward, and the show knows it is running on charm rather than plot. A 7.8 from over sixty thousand ratings, which is generous for a show whose best hour is its first.

title: Extraordinary Attorney Woo
hookNote: Episode 1. The whale and the revolving door do the entire job inside twenty minutes.
endingText: She keeps the job on her own terms, the romance lands softly, and nobody is asked to become someone else.
verdict: The first ten episodes are a warm, specific case-of-the-week show built on a lead performance that deserved every award it got. Then it becomes a corporate conspiracy drama with a love triangle, and the cases stop being about anything. The autism writing is affectionate and sometimes too tidy, and the show is at its best when a case is small and slightly funny. It pulls the finale back together, but the stretch before it drags. Watch it for Park Eun Bin and the whales, and expect the plot to let you down.

title: Extraordinary You
hookNote: Episode 2, when she works out what kind of world she is actually living in.
endingText: It closes the loop it opened, but it lands on feeling rather than on the rules it spent ten episodes teaching you.
verdict: The most inventive premise in teen drama: a girl realises she is a background character in a comic and starts fighting the author for her own scenes. For ten half-hour episodes it is thrilling and the per-episode curve peaks right there, at 9.3. Then it decides it would rather be a first-love romance than a story about authorship, and the last third coasts on sweetness while its own rules go quiet. The lead pair is lovely and the concept deserved a braver back half.

title: Family by Choice
hookNote: Episode 1. The three kids and the makeshift household are established beautifully in the first two hours.
endingText: The family holds together and the romance settles, after a late medical thread that lands as a shortcut.
verdict: The childhood half is one of the best things 2024 produced and the adult half spends sixteen episodes undoing it. Three children raised as siblings by two broken fathers, filmed with real warmth and no sentimentality, and then a love triangle grafted onto the same people once they grow up. Hwang In Youp and Jung Chae Yeon are fine. The younger cast is better. The last four hours reach for illness and estrangement instead of finishing the story they started. Watch the first six with your expectations managed.

title: Fight for My Way
hookNote: Episode 1. The friendship is fully established in the first twenty minutes.
endingText: Both couples land, both careers land, and the final hour is almost entirely epilogue.
verdict: Four friends in their late twenties who are not winning at anything, which is the whole appeal. Park Seo Jun and Kim Ji Won play a friends-to-lovers pair with a twenty-year history, and it is unusually good at the part after they get together, where most romcoms stop trying. The second couple is not filler either, and their fight about marriage is the sharpest writing in it. It sags around episode fourteen when a sports plot needs a villain, and it recovers in time.

title: Flex X Cop
hookNote: Episode 1. A rich heir gets dumped into a violent crimes unit and the tone is locked in immediately.
endingText: The long case resolves, the team stays together, and the last episode is the highest rated of the sixteen.
verdict: The most purely enjoyable Korean drama of 2024 and the one to hand anybody who says procedurals are boring. Every episode is built to be fun: snappy dialogue, a case that actually closes, action staged rather than edited, and a partnership that grows without a romance being forced into it. Ahn Bo Hyun has never been better cast. It is not deep and never pretends to be. Sixteen hours, no filler, no homework.

title: Flower of Evil
hookNote: Episode 2, once the wife starts investigating her own husband. Episode 1 opens with a scene that is hard to sit through.
endingText: The marriage survives the truth and the show deliberately refuses tragedy. It gets there with a device that is close to a cop-out, so the outcome is kind and the last episode is the weakest one.
verdict: A thriller premise carried entirely by a marriage. A man living under a false identity, a wife who works homicide, and the real question is never whether she catches him but what she does with him afterwards. Lee Joon Gi and Moon Chae Won are why it works; the police procedural around them is ordinary and the big reveal arrives early enough that the back half is about consequences instead of suspense. It is tense rather than heavy, and it resolves properly, which this genre rarely manages. One of the few thrillers here you can hand to someone who does not like thrillers.

title: Genie, Make a Wish
hookNote: Episode 1. The wish rules and the cold woman who does not want anything are both established fast, and the ratings never move more than two tenths across thirteen hours.
endingText: A reincarnation ending: the loss is real, and the show spends its last hour arguing it was worth paying.
verdict: A fantasy romcom about a psychopath who cannot feel and a genie who feels everything, and the pairing produces something unexpectedly affecting. The wish rules are clear, the comedy lands, and the show is smart enough to make the female lead's condition clinical rather than cute. The reincarnation ending is a coin toss: the loss is real, and the show argues it was worth paying. A comfort watch with a punch, which is rare.
aliases: All the Love You Wish For

title: Goblin
query: Guardian: The Lonely and Great God
hookNote: Episode 8. Everything before it is mood, rules and comedy, and the buildup is the longest of any show on this site. From episode 8 the per-episode ratings step up and never come back down.
endingText: Fate is honoured rather than cheated, and the cost gets paid in full before the last stretch offers a reunion on new terms.
verdict: The most watched drama in this catalog, and the one whose reputation sits furthest from how it actually plays. A 939-year-old man, the woman who can end him, a grim reaper who forgot his own name, and the best thing in it is not the romance: it is the two men sharing a house and refusing to admit they are friends. The problem is the middle, which is slow to a fault and replays scenes it has already given you, with enough filler in it to have made a tighter twelve episodes. The last two hours then resolve their own rules with a convenience the sixteen hours before them did not earn. Give it eight episodes before you judge it, and expect it to rewatch better than it first watches.

title: Gold Land
hookNote: Episode 5. The ratings jump almost a full point here, which is where the greed stops being a plot and starts being the subject.
endingText: Bleak, and it follows the greed all the way down. Nobody walks out of the last hour with anything intact.
verdict: A greed thriller set at an airport where a smuggling accident turns everyone into a worse version of themselves, and the show follows the descent all the way down. The production is slick, the ratings jump at episode five when the premise stops being a setup and becomes the subject, and the ending is bleak in a way Korean drama rarely commits to. A 7.7 that reflects discomfort rather than disappointment: nobody walks out of the last hour with anything intact.

title: Good Boy
hookNote: Episode 1. Retired Olympians are recruited into a police unit and the tone is set immediately. The structure after that is a loop rather than a build.
endingText: The team wins and the medical thread is resolved much more gently than the setup promised it would be.
verdict: Former national athletes become cops, which is a great premise and a sixteen episode problem. The loop is visible by the fourth hour: the team fights, the team loses badly, the hero absorbs another injury nobody with his diagnosis would survive, the team fights again. Park Bo Gum and Kim So Hyun are both better than the script, Oh Jung Se is enjoying himself, and the action is genuinely well staged. What it lacks is consequence, because the illness that should give the whole thing weight is treated as a pill you take. Fun in three hour doses, exhausting at sixteen.

title: Good Partner
hookNote: Episode 1. The divorce cases and the mentor rivalry are both running inside the first hour.
endingText: The mentorship resolves warmly and the personal case ends without a tidy reconciliation.
verdict: A divorce-law procedural built on a mentor-junior dynamic that is more interesting than the cases they handle. Jang Na Ra and Nam Ji Hyun have a rivalry that evolves into mutual respect without the show having to announce it, and the divorce cases are grounded enough to carry the legal scenes. The personal plot resolves warmly without a tidy reconciliation, which is a rare and correct choice for a show about divorce. Sixteen episodes, competent throughout, and the acting is the reason to stay.

title: Gyeongseong Creature
hookNote: Episode 2, once the hospital becomes the setting rather than a rumour. The pace changes completely there.
endingText: The main thread closes and the two leads get an ending, with one loose thread deliberately left for the sequel.
verdict: A colonial-era monster story that is much better at the colonial era than at the monster. The Gyeongseong of 1945 is built with real money and real detail, the human cruelty inside the hospital lands harder than anything with claws, and Park Seo Jun and Han So Hee are charming enough to carry the slow stretches. The creature work is fine and the plot is thinner than the ten hours it fills. Season one is the one to watch. The sequel is a different show wearing the same title.

title: Gyeongseong Creature Season 2
hookNote: Episode 3, where the present-day case finally has stakes. The first two hours re-establish a premise you already understand.
endingText: The immediate case is settled and the larger one is not. The last scene is an invitation to a third season that has not been ordered.
verdict: Moving to 2024 Seoul strips out everything that made season one worth watching. The period detail is gone, the monster mythology gets explained until it stops being frightening, and the romance is reduced to a memory the show keeps replaying. Seven episodes, one good action set piece, and a plot that runs on coincidence. Han So Hee is doing more work than the script deserves. Skip it unless you need the story closed.

title: He Is Psychometric
hookNote: Episode 1. The building collapse and the ability are established at once.
endingText: The case closes on an act of choosing rather than a chase, and the survivors are left with work still to do.
verdict: A young man who reads memories by touch, chasing a building collapse that everyone involved is lying about. The gimmick is used properly, as a way to withhold context rather than to hand over answers, and the per-episode ratings climb to 9.6 by the finale, which almost nothing else here manages. Jinyoung is better than he needs to be and the four leads actually feel like friends. The romance is the weakest strand and it knows it, keeping it slow and to the side.

title: Head Over Heels
hookNote: Episode 1. A teenage shaman meets the unluckiest boy in school and decides to keep him alive, and the setup is complete in one hour.
endingText: The fate the first half sets up does get dealt with, and the last two hours spend their time somewhere else entirely.
verdict: For eight episodes this is the best young romance of 2025: a high school shaman hiding her work, a boy whose luck is killing him, and a best friend who knows he is losing. Cho Yi Hyun is very good and the supernatural rules are kept simple enough to care about. Then a new character arrives around episode nine, the show hands him the plot, and the ending belongs to a story that has almost nothing to do with the one you started. The fall off is steep and it is the only thing anyone remembers. Watch the first eight, then decide whether you want the rest.

title: Her Private Life
hookNote: Episode 3, once the boss knows and the show stops protecting the secret.
endingText: A family thread resolves gently and the couple ends exactly where the first episode promised.
verdict: A gallery curator running a secret fan site for an idol, and her new boss finds out. It is the most purely pleasant romance in this catalog and the rewatch numbers agree, averaging close to nine out of ten. Park Min Young and Kim Jae Wook get together early and stay together, so the back half runs on a birth-secret subplot nobody needed and the episode curve dips accordingly. Low stakes, high warmth, nothing in it to be nervous about.

title: Hierarchy
hookNote: Episode 1. The transfer student arrives and the revenge plot is stated outright, which is as good as it gets.
endingText: The secret comes out, the punishment is minimal, and the last episode aims at a sequel instead of a conclusion.
verdict: Elite Class in a blazer, and exactly as thin as it looks. Seven episodes of beautiful people in a beautiful school, a revenge plot that forgets its own motive by the fourth hour, and dialogue that explains what the previous scene already showed. Production design is the only department doing its job. The 2024 school drama worth your time is Pyramid Game. This is the one to scroll past.

title: Hometown Cha-Cha-Cha
hookNote: Episode 2, once the village cast is established.
endingText: A late reveal explains the male lead's grief, then everything resolves warmly. No twist ruins it.
verdict: The comfort watch other comfort watches get measured against, and it is honest about being one. The village is the draw, not the couple: eight or nine supporting characters get real arcs and the seaside setting does half the emotional work. It stumbles in the last third, where it manufactures a tragic backstory it does not need and slows right down to deliver it. The leads carry it through anyway. Watch it when you are tired and want something kind that is not stupid.

title: Hospital Playlist
hookNote: Episode 2, when the band and the friendship rhythm take over from the medical cases.
endingText: Season one ends on an open, warm note with the friendships intact. Season two finishes the romances.
verdict: The best hangout show Korea has made, and barely a medical drama at all. Almost nothing happens: five friends in their forties eat, play in a terrible band, and occasionally save a life. It takes two episodes to stop feeling like a slow procedural and then becomes very hard to leave. The patient cases are the weakest part, sentimental and self-contained, and the romances move slowly enough to test you. Season two finishes what this one starts, so plan for both.

title: Hospital Playlist Season 2
hookNote: Episode 1. It restarts inside the same rhythm, so there is nothing to establish and no warm-up to sit through.
endingText: Every romance season one left open gets an answer, the five friendships stay intact, and it closes as a goodbye rather than a cliffhanger.
verdict: Better than season one at the thing you came back for and worse at everything around it. The romances finally move, the band gets more room, and the ensemble is comfortable enough together that the show almost stops being a medical drama at all. The cost is length: twelve episodes at a hundred minutes, with long musical detours and repeated jokes doing work the patient cases used to do. Watch it, then treat the two seasons as one twenty-four episode show, because that is how it was written. The last episode is a proper goodbye, which is rarer than it should be.

title: Hotel del Luna
hookNote: Episode 3, once the hotel staff get histories of their own.
endingText: The central bargain is honoured rather than dodged. It closes gently, but it does close.
verdict: Gorgeous, enormously popular, and structurally a mess. Every frame of the hotel is a designed object and IU's thousand-year-old owner is a great character, but the show never decides whether it is a ghost-of-the-week series or one long tragedy about her past, so both get told at half strength. The staff histories are the best writing in it and arrive too late to fix the pacing. Watch it for the production design, the soundtrack and IU, expect to skim parts of the middle, and know going in that it is sad on purpose.

title: Hyper Knife
hookNote: Episode 3, when the mentor and the protege stop circling and start operating on each other, figuratively and otherwise. Episode 4 is the peak.
endingText: Deliberately ambiguous, which suits the story it is telling and will infuriate anyone who wanted the question settled.
verdict: Two neurosurgeons, one a mentor and one a protege, circling each other for eight episodes of psychological thriller that is more interested in the ethics of genius than the surgeries themselves. Park Eun Bin delivers, the ambiguity of the ending is deliberate, and the show has the confidence to leave the central question unanswered. It will infuriate anyone who wanted closure and satisfy anyone who wanted the argument. A 7.9 that reflects the polarisation rather than the quality.

title: If Wishes Could Kill
hookNote: Episode 1. The app, the wish and the first death all arrive in the opening hour. Episode 6 is the peak.
endingText: The curse is closed and then undercut by a final beat that reopens it for a sequel.
verdict: A supernatural horror about a wish-granting app that kills its users, and the first episode is the best hour Netflix has put out in Korea this year. The curse mechanics are clear, the violence is graphic, and the eight-episode runtime is right for the premise. The ending undercuts itself with a sequel-bait final beat that cheapens the closure the rest of the show earned. A strong horror that does not trust its own ending.

title: If You Wish Upon Me
hookNote: Episode 3, once the hospice wish-granting team is fully assembled.
endingText: Deaths happen and are handled gently. The lead ends the show wanted by people who actively chose him.
verdict: A hospice drama that earns every tear instead of manufacturing them. Ji Chang Wook plays against type as a man who has been unwanted his whole life and it is the best work he has done: quiet, damaged, and never played for charm. The wish-granting premise gives each episode a clean arc, and the found family at the hospice is written with genuine care. The second half is weaker than the first and the romance is an afterthought, but the final stretch is devastating because the show spent fourteen hours teaching you to love a character the world did not love.

title: Itaewon Class
hookNote: Episode 3, once the bar opens and the crew assembles.
endingText: The underdog wins on his own terms and the revenge lands. The time skip, the love triangle and the female lead's arc are where it comes apart, and the last quarter plays like a different series.
verdict: The first eight episodes are a genuinely angry underdog story and the last eight are a business fantasy with a love triangle. Park Seo Joon's stubborn ex-convict opening a bar to ruin the man who destroyed his family is a great engine, and the staff he assembles is the best part of the show. Then the villain turns stupid, the lead's obsessive devotion stops making sense, and the finale hands out wins it has not earned. Worth it for the first half and the cast. Stop needing the revenge to be satisfying and it goes down much easier.

title: It's Okay, That's Love
hookNote: Episode 3, once the housemates are all under one roof and the household becomes the setting.
endingText: Illness is managed, not cured. The couple ends together with the work ongoing, which is the entire argument.
verdict: Ten years before It's Okay to Not Be Okay, this did the same job better. A novelist and a psychiatrist share a house, and the illness at the centre is something to live with rather than a plot device, which the show manages while still being funny. Zo In Sung and Kong Hyo Jin are the most adult couple in this catalog. The 2014 production shows in the needle drops, one stretch of the back half is heavy handed, and the reveal it builds to rewards patience rather than surprising you. It ends with the work ongoing, which is the entire argument.

title: It's Okay to Not Be Okay
query: It's Okay to Not Be Okay
hookNote: Episode 3, when the brothers' history starts opening up.
endingText: All three leads end up healthier than they started. The road trip finale is unambiguously kind.
verdict: Gorgeous, deliberately theatrical, and about a third longer than its story. The fairytale framing and the production design are the point, and the two leads plus the brother make one of the best written trios in the genre. Then it loses its nerve and swaps the psychiatric ward material for a thriller plot about a nurse that adds nothing. Heavy going in the middle and genuinely restorative by the end. Worth it if you want a drama about caretaking rather than a romance.

title: Jeongnyeon: The Star Is Born
hookNote: Episode 4, once the troupe accepts her and the rivalry has something at stake.
endingText: The dream is reached on modest terms and the rivalry resolves warmly.
verdict: A 1950s story about a Mokpo girl fighting her way into a women's traditional theatre troupe, with a sapphic subtext that is the actual text for anyone paying attention. The casting is strong, the musical numbers are genuine, and the rivalry between the leads drives the twelve episodes better than the romance. The censorship of the source material's same-sex relationship is visible and frustrating, and the back half is weaker than the front. Worth it for the performances and the period detail, less so for the courage the adaptation did not have.

title: Just Between Lovers
hookNote: Episode 3, once the shared history behind the collapse becomes clear.
endingText: The grief is not resolved so much as carried together. They end up choosing each other in daylight.
verdict: The quietest disaster melodrama here and the one that earns its recovery. Two survivors of the same building collapse meet a decade later, and the drama is patient enough to let them be avoidant, unpleasant and physically in pain long before it lets them be in love. Lee Jun Ho is the surprise, doing more with silence than most leads manage with a monologue. The construction conspiracy running underneath is functional at best and the first two episodes are grey and slow. From episode nine on it is as good as this genre gets.

title: Juvenile Justice
hookNote: Episode 1, and it is the hardest case in the series. If you can take episode 1 you can take the rest.
endingText: Nothing about the system is fixed. The judge stays in the job, which the show treats as the only available victory.
verdict: Episode one is the hardest hour of the entire ten, and if you can survive it you can survive everything that follows. Kim Hye Soo plays a judge who despises juvenile offenders and then has to sit in a court where every case is a child, and the writing is smart enough never to soften her or let anyone off easy. There is no romance, no comic relief, and no outcome that feels like justice. Ten episodes on Netflix, no filler, no padding, and it leaves a bruise.

title: Karma
hookNote: Episode 3, once the separate timelines start colliding and the structure becomes the point of the whole thing.
endingText: Everybody pays, in the order the title promises. Nobody is redeemed and nobody is spared.
verdict: Six episodes, no filler, no mercy. The multi-timeline structure is the whole point: three stories of greed and desperation collide in the order the title promises, and nobody is redeemed. It is dark, efficient, and genuinely tragic in the final stretch. The brevity is a virtue: there is nothing to cut and nothing to add, which is almost unheard of in Korean drama.

title: King the Land
hookNote: Episode 1. The heir and the smiling hotel clerk meet in the first twenty minutes and the show never complicates that.
endingText: Every obstacle folds in the last two hours and the couple gets the ending the first episode promised.
verdict: The archetype romcom of 2023, and it took the crown from Business Proposal by copying its blueprint exactly: chaebol heir, hardworking employee, hotel setting, bickering, a boardroom subplot nobody watches for. Lee Jun Ho and Yoona are effortless together and the production is expensive in the way that makes a show easy to put on. It also has no plot: an 8.3 aggregate from 102,000 ratings sits against a written-review average of 6.6 and a rewatch score of 4.6, which is what an empty pleasant show looks like in numbers. Watch it when you want nothing to happen for sixteen hours.

title: Kingdom
hookNote: Episode 2, once the outbreak reaches the village and the scale is clear.
endingText: Six hours in it stops on a deliberate cliff with the crisis still spreading, so it needs what comes after it.
verdict: Zombies in Joseon, and the political half is better than the horror half. Kim Eun Hee uses the plague as an argument about a court that starves its own people, so the horror lands because the hunger does, and six fifty-minute episodes means nothing is padded. It looks better than most Korean film, the crown prince is a real character rather than a hero, and the gore earns its rating. It ends mid-story, which is the only real caution.

title: Knight Flower
hookNote: Episode 2, once the masked night work and the household deception start colliding.
endingText: The villain falls, the widow keeps her freedom, and the household ends up on her side.
verdict: A sageuk action comedy where a Joseon widow fights crime at night and plays dutiful daughter-in-law by day, and the tonal balance works. Lee Ha Nee is magnetic in the lead, the comedy is genuine, and the twelve episodes move fast. The mystery underneath the action is weaker than the character work above it, and the romance is a pleasant addition rather than the engine. Light, fun, and exactly as long as it needs to be.

title: Law and the City
hookNote: Episode 4, once the five friends stop being introduced and start being lived with. Nothing here is designed to grab you.
endingText: No big finish. It closes on the same dinner table it opened on, which is the entire point of the twelve hours.
verdict: A slice-of-life legal drama about five lawyer friends who share a dinner table, and the show is deliberately designed not to grab you. The cases are realistic, the relationships are warm, and nothing here is trying to be exciting. The 7.9 rating is from people who wanted a thriller and got a hangout show, which is the show's fault for marketing and the show's strength for existing. If you want Korean Friends with law degrees, this is it.

title: Law School
hookNote: Episode 1. A professor dies in a mock-trial classroom before the opening credits.
endingText: The death is explained, the students graduate, and the professor is cleared.
verdict: How to Get Away with Murder rebuilt in a Korean law school with better acting and tighter plotting. A professor dies in a mock trial classroom before the credits roll and the sixteen episodes never let the tension drop for long. Kim Bum and Ryu Hye Young lead a student ensemble that actually earns screen time rather than stealing it, and the legal mechanics are plausible enough to carry the twists. The first quarter is dry, and the payoff is worth the patience.

title: Life on Mars
hookNote: Episode 2, once the 1988 precinct stops being a joke to him and starts being a place.
endingText: The nature of the 1988 world is explained. Whether that explanation satisfies you is genuinely a coin flip.
verdict: The best OCN procedural and the only remake here that improves on its source. A data-driven detective wakes up in 1988 with a squad that closes cases by intimidation, and the show mines that gap for comedy before turning it into something much colder about what policing used to be. Jung Kyung Ho is superb, the individual cases are strong, and there is no romance slowing it down. The finale explains the 1988 world, and whether that explanation lands decides your rating: it is either the point or a cop-out. The last two hours are the weakest and it is still a straight recommendation.

title: Light Shop
hookNote: Episode 5, where the strangers turn out to be one story and the horror framing shows what it has actually been doing.
endingText: It resolves, and it resolves gently. What looked like a ghost story turns out to be about the people left behind.
verdict: Eight episodes that pretend to be horror for four and then hand you a grief drama. Kang Full wrote it, Kim Hee Won directed it, and the structural turn in the middle is the best built reveal Disney+ has aired in years. The scares before it are thin and the ensemble is too big for the runtime, so the first half feels like homework. The fifth hour makes the other seven worth it. Read nothing about it before you start.

title: Little Women
hookNote: Episode 1. The money goes missing inside the first hour and the show never slows down again.
endingText: The sisters come out of it and the money question gets a clean, satisfying answer. The last stretch is where it wobbles: the pace that carried the first nine episodes goes slack, and one relationship the show spent all season building never actually resolves.
verdict: Rated modestly and written brilliantly, which is the reverse of the usual problem here. Three poor sisters, seventy billion won, and a political family with an orchid obsession, and it plays as a thriller rather than a family drama. Kim Go Eun and Wi Ha Joon are good, and Uhm Ji Won's villain is one of the best in the catalog. The last two episodes get tangled and the youngest sister's plot gets shortchanged, and neither ruins it. If you liked the plotting in The Glory, this is better plotted.

title: Live
hookNote: Episode 3, after the training arc ends.
endingText: No tidy bow. The station survives, the cast is battered but intact, and one thread is deliberately left open.
verdict: Eighteen episodes about patrol officers filing paperwork, breaking up drunks and getting screamed at by the public, and one of the best things Noh Hee Kyung has written. No genius profiler, no serial killer: the crimes are small, domestic and mostly unresolvable, and the show cares more about pay grades and bureaucracy than arrests. Lee Kwang Soo is career-best here, which nobody expects going in. It is episodic to a fault and the romance is barely there. At 9,500 ratings it is the most overlooked entry in this catalog.

title: Lost
hookNote: Episode 4, when the two leads stop circling each other and finally talk. The first three are deliberately bleak.
endingText: Nobody is rescued and nothing is fixed. Both leads decide to keep going, and the show treats that as enough.
verdict: A drama about two people who are failing at life and know it, told at the pace of actually failing at life. Jeon Do Yeon and Ryu Jun Yeol play their exhaustion as something physical rather than decorative, and the writing never offers them a shortcut. It is beautifully shot, barely plotted, and requires a tolerance for stillness that most dramas never ask for. The ending is hopeful in the narrowest sense: nothing is fixed, and staying alive is the accomplishment.

title: Love Next Door
hookNote: Episode 3, once the reason she quit her job and came home stops being a punchline.
endingText: Both leads resolve their own crises before the romance closes, and the families land somewhere warm.
verdict: Childhood friends, meddling mothers, and a burnout story hiding inside a neighbourhood romcom. Jung So Min is excellent as a woman who cannot admit she has broken down, and the show is at its best in the quiet scenes with her mother rather than the shouting ones. The middle pads itself with misunderstandings and the second-lead subplots go nowhere. Comfort viewing with a real subject underneath it, which is more than most sixteen episode romcoms manage.

title: Love Scout
hookNote: Episode 2, when the headhunter and the single father CEO start actually working together rather than sparring about it.
endingText: Clean and warm. Both careers and the relationship land, and it declines the wedding scene the genre usually insists on.
verdict: A boss-employee romcom that does everything the genre asks and does it with genuine warmth. The single-father CEO and the headhunter have chemistry built on mutual competence rather than bickering, and the twelve episodes never manufacture a crisis the characters cannot solve by talking. Clean, warm, and the kind of show that skips the wedding scene because the relationship already proved itself. An 8.4 from over sixty thousand ratings, and it is the best pure romcom of 2025.

title: Lovely Runner
hookNote: Episode 2, the first jump back. Be warned: the lead's fan-girl register in the first two episodes is a lot to take, and it settles around episode 6.
endingText: Every timeline debt gets paid and the loop closes on the version of events you were rooting for. The route there is repetitive by design, and a sizeable minority think the story should have finished around episode 8
verdict: An 8.9 aggregate from a hundred thousand ratings, and written reviews that average about a three. Both are correct. Episodes one to eight are the best pure comfort romance of 2024, with a time travel hook that works and a lead pair worth the noise. After the second jump it starts bending its own rules to keep the couple apart, the plot holes stop being ignorable, and the last stretch repeats itself enough to undo the goodwill. Watch the first half without hesitation. Whether you finish depends on how much you forgive a show for loving its premise more than its logic.

title: Marry My Husband
hookNote: Episode 1. She dies, wakes up ten years earlier, and starts redirecting her own murder inside the first hour.
endingText: The revenge lands, both villains get exactly what the setup promised, and the couple ends together with no late twist.
verdict: A revenge fantasy with the pacing of a thriller and no interest whatsoever in subtlety. The premise is trash and it is executed with total conviction: every trap is set up and paid off, and the show never makes its heroine wait for permission. Song Ha Yoon's villain is the best performance in it, a sweetness that curdles on camera. The added ex-fiancee subplot is dead weight and episode twelve stalls badly. Sixteen hours of clean, mean satisfaction.

title: Mask Girl
hookNote: Episode 3, when the lead is recast and the show reveals it is a relay race across three actresses rather than one story.
endingText: It closes the loop on all three chapters. One character gets something like grace, and nobody gets forgiveness.
verdict: Three actresses play one woman across twenty years of humiliation, violence and internet fame, and the handover between them is the most interesting formal idea in a 2023 Korean series. Lee Han Byeol, Nana and Go Hyun Jung are all excellent, and the writing is cruellest to the characters it understands best. It is also relentlessly bleak, explicit about bodies and appearance in a way that will put many off, and the final chapter reaches for redemption it has not earned. Seven hours, no comfort, real ambition.

title: Melo Movie
hookNote: Episode 7 is the best hour in the run, which is very late for a ten episode show. Before that it is atmosphere and film references.
endingText: Grief is not solved and the couple is. It ends on a working film set and a small, earned peace.
verdict: Two people who love and resent cinema for opposite reasons, a critic and a director, circling each other through a decade of grief. The second story, an older brother and the woman he could not stay with, is stronger than the main one and knows it. Choi Woo Shik and Park Bo Young are quietly excellent and the show is beautifully shot. It is also slow in a way that reads as unfinished rather than restrained. This is a mood you either sink into or bounce off. Watch it late at night or not at all.

title: Memories of the Alhambra
hookNote: Episode 1. The game and the first duel arrive fast.
endingText: It withholds a resolution and finishes on a note that reads as either open or unfinished, depending on how much patience you have left.
verdict: An augmented-reality game bleeding into Granada, and for twelve episodes it is the most exciting high-concept thriller here: real rules, real dread, and Hyun Bin very good as a man who cannot tell what is rendered. Then Song Jae Jung runs out of ideas for her own premise, the last four hours swap logic for mystery, and the finale rates lowest of the run. Park Shin Hye is stranded in a part that mostly waits. Watch it for the middle stretch and set your expectations for the ending now.

title: Mercy for None
hookNote: Episode 1. A brother is dead, a man walks back into the organisation he left, and the violence starts immediately. Seven episodes of forty minutes with nothing spare.
endingText: The debt gets paid and the payment takes everything with it. Noir keeps its own rules to the last frame.
verdict: Seven episodes of pure noir: a brother is dead, a man walks back into the gang he left, and the violence starts immediately. The fights are spectacular and the plotting is deliberately simple, because the point is the descent rather than the mystery. Style over substance, and the style is genuinely good. A 8.3 from nearly forty thousand ratings, and the people who wanted depth instead of choreography are the ones who scored it lower.

title: Misaeng: Incomplete Life
hookNote: Episode 2, once the sales team starts treating him like a person rather than a filing error.
endingText: The company never rewards him fairly. He leaves on his own terms, with the people who mattered.
verdict: The best workplace drama Korea has made and the least escapist thing in this catalog. A Go prodigy with no degree lands an internship at a trading company, and the show is about spreadsheets, photocopiers and the exact mechanics of a hierarchy grinding a person down. There is no romance, no villain, and no promotion that fixes anything. Twenty episodes at eighty minutes does drag through the contract arc. If you have ever been the least qualified person in the room, this stops feeling like television.

title: Miss Night and Day
hookNote: Episode 1. The overnight ageing happens immediately and the double life starts with it.
endingText: The curse resolves, the job is kept, and the romance closes without complications.
verdict: A body-swap comedy where a twentysomething job seeker ages into her fifties overnight, and the show uses the premise for workplace comedy rather than the fantasy it promises. Lee Jung Eun and Jung Eun Ji split the lead convincingly, and the prosecutor love interest is charming without being the point. It runs sixteen episodes, which is four more than the premise can carry, and the mystery behind the ageing is the weakest thread. Fun, light, and forgettable in the way pleasant romcoms are allowed to be.
aliases: She Is Different Day and Night
A Woman With Different Day and Night
The Girl Who Is Different from Day to Night
The Woman Who Is Different by Day and Night

title: Moon Lovers: Scarlet Heart Ryeo
hookNote: Episode 5. The first four are genuinely choppy because of heavy re-editing. Push through them anyway.
endingText: The throne is won and the love is lost. The final episode is built to hurt and it succeeds.
verdict: An 8.7 from ninety six thousand ratings, and written reviews average barely a six. Nothing else here splits that hard. The first four episodes are genuinely badly assembled after heavy re-editing, and they are the reason it gets dropped. What survives is Lee Joon Gi giving the performance of his career and a court tragedy that does not blink at the end. It is long, it is cruel, and it rewatches worse than almost anything in this catalog because the pleasure is entirely in the hurt. Start it only if you want to be wrecked, and push past episode four.

title: Moonlight Drawn by Clouds
hookNote: Episode 1. The disguise and the meeting are both set up immediately.
endingText: The political threat clears and the couple gets a warm, uncomplicated last episode.
verdict: A cross-dressing eunuch, a crown prince, and the lightest touch any Joseon romance in this catalog manages. Park Bo Gum and Kim Yoo Jung are teenagers playing teenagers and the first ten episodes are close to perfect comfort television. It also has a politics plot it does not care about, and once that plot takes over around episode eleven the ratings sag and stay sagged. Watch the front half for the romance and forgive the back half for the coup.

title: Mouse
hookNote: Episode 2, once the killer and the two men chasing him are locked into the same story.
endingText: It answers its central question completely and charges the lead for it, then closes on a legislative flourish that argues something much uglier than the story needed.
verdict: An 8.9 from 45,000 ratings on a twenty-episode thriller whose per-episode scores never drop below 8.4, and the acting is the reason: Lee Seung Gi has to play two people in one body and does it with posture as much as face. The structure is genuinely ambitious and the central reveal reframes everything in front of it. It is also badly overlong, and the editing misleads for its own sake, showing scenes that did not happen without giving you the tools to doubt them. Written reviews rate the story a full point below the acting, and the last episode then argues a position on who deserves to be born that the sixteen hours before it never earned. Remarkable performance, compromised show.

title: Move to Heaven
hookNote: Episode 1 already tells you exactly what the show is.
endingText: An unlikely family is properly formed by the end. Grief stays grief, but it is carried by more than one person.
verdict: Ten episodes, one job, and the cleanest premise on the site: two men clear out the homes of the dead and find out who lived there. Every episode is a life nobody attended to, and the show handles them with much less sentiment than that sounds like. The uncle and nephew carry it, and Tang Joon Sang is remarkable. It will make you cry in most episodes, which is a warning and not a boast. Nothing else here does grief this plainly.

title: Moving
hookNote: Episode 7, when the show stops being about three kids at school and hands the whole middle stretch to their parents.
endingText: Twenty hours of setup get paid off in a long, brutal final confrontation, and it lands on relief rather than loss.
verdict: Kang Full adapted his own webtoon and the result is the best thing Disney+ has made in Korea. The first six hours are a high school superpower story with a good sense of humour, and then it becomes a 1990s spy melodrama about the parents, which is where it gets great. It is twenty episodes and it feels like it: the middle sags whenever the plot parks the kids to service another flashback, and the violence is graphic enough to matter. Watch it for Ryu Seung Ryong and Han Hyo Joo, and for an action finale that most Korean productions cannot afford.

title: Mr. Plankton
hookNote: Episode 1. The diagnosis and the kidnapped bride both land immediately, so the road trip starts at once.
endingText: It ends the way the setup promises it will. The last episode is gentle about it and never pretends otherwise.
verdict: A terminal illness road comedy that is much funnier than that sentence suggests and much less moving than it wants to be. Woo Do Hwan is genuinely good as a man working hard at being unlovable, and Lee You Mi matches him. The problem is structural: ten episodes of two people bickering across Korea while the show withholds the one conversation they need to have. Oh Jung Se steals every scene he gets. Worth it if you want to cry and can stand being steered into it.

title: Mr. Queen
hookNote: Episode 1. A modern chef wakes up as a Joseon queen inside twenty minutes.
endingText: The body-swap is resolved without cruelty and the palace politics land in the leads favour.
verdict: The funniest sageuk since the genre existed and the most committed body-swap comedy Korea has produced. Shin Hye Sun plays a modern male chef trapped in a Joseon queen's body with physical comedy that deserves awards and never got them. The palace politics underneath the comedy are surprisingly competent, the romance actually works despite the premise, and twenty episodes is somehow not too many. An 8.9 from nearly eighty thousand ratings, and the number is honest.

title: Mr. Sunshine
hookNote: Episode 5, once all three men circling her are in play. The opening hours are a history lesson, and the real barrier is the writing register: the dialogue is elliptical and the flashbacks last seconds, and that is where it either has you or loses you.
endingText: It is a story about the years before an occupation. Very little is spared, and the show never pretends otherwise.
verdict: Twenty-four episodes at eighty minutes, the most expensive looking thing here, and it does not respect your time. Kim Eun Sook writing Korea under Japanese pressure in the 1900s produces extraordinary images and about six hours that could be cut without losing anything. Lee Byung Hun is magnetic, and the two men orbiting the noblewoman are better served than the romance is. It is a nationalist tragedy that ends where it has to, so do not go in wanting comfort. Watch it for the scale, and be prepared to skip.

title: My Dearest
hookNote: Episode 2, once the war arrives and the tone hardens permanently.
endingText: It is technically a happy ending, arrived at through twenty-one episodes of loss. You will not feel unscathed.
verdict: A wartime love story set during the Qing invasion that hits as hard as its historical setting promises. The first ten episodes are a slow-burn romance with real chemistry, and then the war arrives and the show stops being gentle permanently. Namgoong Min and Ahn Eun Jin sell the separation across twenty-one episodes, which is a structural gamble that pays off because the writing trusts silence over dialogue. It is technically a happy ending, arrived at through so much loss that it does not feel like one.

title: My Demon
hookNote: Episode 7, where the contract stops being a gag and the demon actually has something to lose.
endingText: The curse is resolved on the show's own soft terms and the couple ends up together with the cost quietly waived.
verdict: A demon loses his powers, a cynical heiress becomes the human battery he needs, and they sign a marriage contract. Kim You Jung is very good and Song Kang looks the part, and the first four hours are a genuinely fun supernatural romcom. Then the plot runs out and the show fills nine more hours with an inheritance war, a killer nobody cares about and a magic system that changes rules whenever the romance needs it. An 8.3 from 105,000 ratings against a 5.0 written-review average and a 3.3 rewatch score: the gap is the biggest in the 2023 slate for a reason.

title: My ID Is Gangnam Beauty
hookNote: Episode 1. The surgery and the first day of class are both done inside the hour.
endingText: The couple lands cleanly, and the wider question about being looked at is left open on purpose.
verdict: A campus romance about a woman who had plastic surgery to stop being bullied and finds the judgement waiting on the other side.
