It is sharper about beauty standards than its 7.6 aggregate suggests, and written reviews rate it more than a point higher, which is the honest split: a good drama with a blank male lead. Cha Eun Woo is cast for his face and directed to stand still, so Im Soo Hyang carries every scene that matters. The bullying strand gets a real ending rather than a redemption arc, which is rarer than it should be.

title: My Liberation Notes
hookNote: Episode 3, once Mr Gu starts drinking with Mi-jeong. Before that it is deliberately airless.
endingText: Nobody is saved by a plot twist. Each sibling walks out of Sanpo carrying less, and the final scene is a quiet reunion rather than a wedding.
verdict: Sixteen hours of three siblings commuting, and the slowest thing here by a distance. The first four episodes are close to nothing happening, and then the real subject arrives: not romance, but the specific exhaustion of a life that is fine and unbearable at the same time. Son Suk Ku's drunk stranger and Kim Ji Won's worship line are why this page exists. The brother's story never resolves and the ending is deliberately unfinished. Do not start it looking for comfort, and do not start it tired.

title: My Love from Another Star
hookNote: Episode 3, once she moves in next door and the bickering starts.
endingText: The impossible gap gets solved with a piece of invented physics. Sweet, slightly silly, and definitely not tragic.
verdict: The drama that set the template every 2010s romcom then copied, which is also why it has aged the most. Jun Ji Hyun is the reason it works: vain, loud, wrong about everything and impossible to look away from, while the alien opposite her is mostly a straight man with superpowers. Twenty-one episodes is at least four too many, the middle replays its own beats, and the invented physics that resolves the ending is silly. It is still the most fun 2013 has to offer, and Cheon Song Yi is the best comic female lead here.

title: My Mister
hookNote: Episode 4 is the turn. Before that it just looks bleak.
endingText: Nobody is rescued by luck. Both leads walk away lighter than they arrived, and the last scene is a small kindness, not a reunion.
verdict: Written reviews rate it above everything else in this catalog, and it is also the hardest watch here. Two people at the bottom of their lives, one middle aged and hollowed out, one young and criminal, and the drama refuses to make either of them charming about it. The first three episodes are grey and slow enough to lose you; from episode four it is unmatched. There is no romance in the way the poster implies, and that is the point. If you watch one Korean drama for the writing, make it this one.

title: My Name
hookNote: Episode 1. The father dies in the first fifteen minutes and the deal is struck immediately.
endingText: She gets the truth and the revenge. Almost nobody she cared about is left to share it with.
verdict: Eight episodes, one revenge, and the most visceral fight choreography Netflix has funded in Korea. Han So Hee plays a woman who sacrifices her identity to find her father's killer and the show never once pretends she will get it back intact. The plot is thin and predictable, the twist is visible from episode two, and none of that matters because the physicality and the grief are genuine. It costs exactly the right number of hours and does not waste a single one.

title: Mystic Pop-up Bar
hookNote: Episode 1. The bar, the debt and the rules are all on the table immediately.
endingText: The 500-year debt is settled and the found family gets a proper goodbye rather than a tragic one.
verdict: A fantasy procedural with a found family at its centre that is warmer and funnier than the premise suggests. Hwang Jung Eum runs a pojangmacha that resolves grudges in people's dreams, and the episodic cases are better than the mythology arc that connects them. Twelve episodes, no padding, and a 500-year backstory that earns its reveal in the final stretch. The comedy is broad but never cruel, and the ending is a proper goodbye rather than a tragic one.

title: Navillera
hookNote: Episode 2, the first proper lesson. It is a two-hander from there.
endingText: Time does what time does. The final stretch is a gift rather than a rescue.
verdict: A 70-year-old retired postman decides to learn ballet and the show treats the decision with complete seriousness. Song Kang and Park In Hwan play the generational friendship with a gentleness that never tips into sentimentality, and the show is smart enough to give both of them a full arc rather than making the elder a prop for the younger. It is bittersweet where it needs to be: time does what time does, and the final stretch is a gift rather than a rescue. An 8.9 on MDL and one of the rare times the aggregate undersells the show.

title: Nine Puzzles
hookNote: Episode 1. A profiler is the prime suspect in her own uncle's murder, and the puzzle cards start arriving immediately.
endingText: The culprit is guessable and the aftermath is not. The last two hours hit considerably harder than the mystery does.
verdict: A profiler-detective thriller where the profiler is the prime suspect in her own uncle's murder, and the premise is strong enough to carry eleven episodes. The mystery is guessable and the aftermath is not, which is the right way around: the last two hours hit harder than the puzzle does. Solid craft, a strong female lead, and a 8.4 that reflects competence rather than greatness.

title: No Gain No Love
hookNote: Episode 1. The fake wedding scheme is proposed and accepted inside the first hour.
endingText: The contract becomes real and both leads get the promotion, the family and the ending they wanted.
verdict: Shin Min Ah plays a woman who calculates the value of every relationship, which is a good premise the show only half commits to. The first six episodes are sharp about money and pettiness. The last six trade that for standard romcom beats and a sister subplot that eats the runtime. Kim Young Dae is charming and badly underwritten. Pleasant, forgettable, and about four episodes too long.

title: Notes from the Last Row
query: The Boy in the Last Row
hookNote: Episode 2, when the writing lessons turn into something the professor cannot stop reading. Six episodes, no filler.
endingText: It refuses clean closure on purpose. One man's downfall is total, the other's motive is left for you to argue about.
verdict: Six episodes, two actors, and a writing-mentor relationship that turns into something the professor cannot control. The premise is theatrical, the pacing is patient, and the show has the confidence to refuse clean closure. One man's downfall is total, the other's motive is left for you to argue about, and the six hours earn every minute of ambiguity. A small, sharp show that asks you to sit with discomfort.
aliases: The Boy in the Last Row

title: Nothing Uncovered
hookNote: Episode 1. The body and the reporter's own exposure both arrive in the opening hour, which is the high point.
endingText: The murder is solved and the reporter's life is not put back together.
verdict: A thriller about a reporter whose show exposes villains until the villain is her own husband, and the premise is better than the execution. Kim Ha Neul is miscast and Jang Seung Jo is not: the show is at its best when he is on screen and at its weakest when it asks her to carry the investigation alone. The ending is the best part, which is unusual for a show this uneven. A 7.4 from eight thousand ratings, and the number is accurate.
aliases: Let's Get Caught by the Neck
Let Me Grab You by the Collar

title: Oh My Ghost Clients
hookNote: Episode 1. A labour consultant starts seeing the workers who died on the job, and the case of the week format is running by the end of the hour.
endingText: Heartwarming and complete, with the labour cases closed one at a time and the final two hours the heaviest in the run.
verdict: A labour-law comedy with a supernatural twist: a consultant starts seeing the workers who died on the job, and the case-of-the-week format gives each ghost a proper sendoff. The comedy is warm rather than sharp, the final two hours are the heaviest in the run, and the ten episodes never outstay their welcome. A solid mid-tier show that does exactly what it promises.

title: One Spring Night
hookNote: Episode 4, once both families are involved. Before that it is glances and pharmacy small talk.
endingText: Two adults leave the wrong lives on their own timetable. Undramatic, and earned.
verdict: Thirty-two half hours of two adults slowly leaving the wrong lives, from the director of Something in the Rain and without that show's second-half collapse. Almost nothing happens on purpose: it is built from small conversations, family pressure and the logistics of ending a four-year relationship you are already out of. Han Ji Min and Jung Hae In are excellent, and the discarded boyfriend is the best written character in it. If you need plot this will bore you flat. If you want a romance whose obstacle is other people's expectations rather than a villain, nothing else here is close.

title: Our Beloved Summer
hookNote: Episode 3, once the documentary footage starts cutting between who they were and who they are.
endingText: They get back together properly, each having done the work separately first.
verdict: Beautiful, well acted, and about four episodes of story. Two former high school sweethearts get dragged back in front of a documentary camera, and the interview format is a genuinely good device for showing two people lie about the same events. The problem is that the breakup was never really about anything, so the reconciliation cannot be either, and the gap gets filled with mood, lighting and a second lead subplot that goes nowhere. Choi Woo Shik is excellent. Watch it for the atmosphere, not the plot, and expect to watch it once.

title: Our Blues
hookNote: Episode 3 closes the first chapter and sells the anthology format.
endingText: Every storyline lands somewhere gentle. One storyline stays sad on purpose, but it is signposted long before it arrives.
verdict: A Jeju Island anthology where every chapter is a different couple or family and the connective tissue is the island itself. Noh Hee Kyung writes middle-aged characters with a patience the genre almost never grants them, and the ensemble, particularly Lee Byung Hun and Shin Min Ah, does career-best work. Twenty episodes is a lot, the anthology format means some chapters land harder than others, and the teen pregnancy arc is polarising. Warm, melancholic, and unconcerned with being exciting.

title: Our Sticky Love
hookNote: Episode 7, if you get that far. Nothing before it raises a stake or asks the amnesia premise to do any work.
endingText: Everyone is forgiven and everyone is paired off, with a fan service coda in place of a resolution.
verdict: An amnesia romcom that takes seven episodes to raise a single stake and then resolves everything with a fan-service coda instead of a proper ending. The rural village is charming, the lead chemistry is present, and nothing else here justifies twelve hours. The 8.2 is from completionists: the first-episode dropout rate tells the real story.

title: Our Universe
hookNote: Episode 1 is the best hour and the ratings fall off a cliff from there, bottoming out around episodes 8 and 9. There is no later hook.
endingText: The orphaned nephew, who is supposedly the whole subject, gets his story crammed into the last two hours and then resolved warmly.
verdict: A family dramedy about two in-laws raising an orphaned nephew, and the nephew's story, which is supposedly the subject, is crammed into the last two hours. The male lead's subplot and friends are the best thing in it, the female lead is badly written, and the 7.5 rating is earned. The first episode is the high point and the curve falls from there.

title: Our Unwritten Seoul
hookNote: Episode 1, where the swap happens and both sisters immediately have to live with it. The ratings open at their highest and drift down from there.
endingText: Both sisters end up living their own lives rather than each other's, and the last hour is deliberately quiet about it.
verdict: Twins swap lives, one in Seoul and one in the countryside, and the show is much less interested in the mix up than in what each of them was hiding from. Park Bo Young plays both and the two performances are properly distinct even when her default mannerisms show through. What it does well is the weight underneath a soft surface: this is about losing yourself to a life you agreed to, and it does not resolve that cheaply. It is also eighty minutes an episode of a story that would breathe better at sixty, and the rewatch appetite is low. One watch, worth it.

title: Parasyte: The Grey
hookNote: Episode 1. The infection and the uneasy truce inside one body are both established inside forty minutes.
endingText: The hunt closes and the central bargain resolves, with the last scene setting up more.
verdict: Six episodes, no fat, and a genuinely clever twist on the manga: the parasite in her hand can only surface for fifteen minutes at a time, which turns every fight into a countdown. Jeon So Nee plays two things at once and never blurs them, and Koo Kyo Hwan is the reason to stay. The task force scenes are stock and the gore is heavy enough to matter if that bothers you. Best Korean science fiction horror on Netflix, and it respects your evening.

title: Perfect Crown
hookNote: Episode 1, and it keeps climbing to episode 3. The contract is signed early and the show never stalls waiting for the leads to admit anything.
endingText: Happy and a little rushed. The couple lands cleanly while two antagonist threads get tidied away in the space of a few minutes.
verdict: A constitutional monarchy in modern Korea, a chaebol heiress who wants a title, a prince who has nothing but one, and a contract marriage between them. It is silly, it is glossy, and it is the most competent straight romcom in years, because it commits: no reluctant will-they, no half-episode misunderstandings, and a second couple worth the screen time. IU is doing exactly what she is good at and Byeon Woo Seok is better here than in Lovely Runner, mostly because the part asks him to be still. The script is thin and the villains are cardboard. Start it knowing that and it delivers everything it promises.

title: Phantom Lawyer
hookNote: Episode 1. Ghost clients, one reluctant lawyer, case of the week. The middle stretch is flat and the last two hours are the strongest.
endingText: The obvious happy ending, reached without much resistance from anything the sixteen hours set up.
verdict: A ghost-client legal comedy that is cozy, predictable, and exactly as long as it should not be. Sixteen episodes is far too many for a case-of-the-week show with no central mystery, and the middle stretch is flat. The final two hours are the strongest, the leads are likeable, and the 8.2 reflects a show that people finished rather than a show that challenged them.

title: Prison Playbook
hookNote: Episode 2, once the cell mates are introduced properly.
endingText: Almost everyone gets a fair landing and the last episode is openly sentimental about it.
verdict: The highest rated entry in this catalog, from the director of Reply 1988, and it works the same way: a cell block full of people you learn to like. A baseball pitcher is jailed, and the show is a comedy about routine, hierarchy and small kindnesses, interrupted by one episode of real violence to remind you where you are. It is a soft version of prison and the pitcher is the least interesting man in his own cell. The first episode is the worst one; from the second the ensemble takes over. Almost everybody gets a fair landing, which is why it rewatches so easily.

title: Pyramid Game
hookNote: Episode 1. The monthly popularity vote and the class ranking it creates are laid out immediately.
endingText: The system comes down and the cost of bringing it down is paid on screen. Nobody walks away clean.
verdict: A girls' school ranked by anonymous monthly vote, which is the sharpest structural idea in any Korean school drama. Ten episodes that treat bullying as politics rather than melodrama, so every alliance shifts for a reason and the hierarchy is always one vote from collapse. Bo Na and Jang Da A are both excellent and neither is asked to be likeable. It is hard to watch in places. If The Glory was too baroque for you, this is the cold version.

title: Queen of Tears
hookNote: Episode 4, when the in-law hierarchy flips. The chaebol scaffolding takes a while to pay off.
endingText: It threatens the worst for twelve hours and then pulls back. A late epilogue reframes the whole marriage kindly.
verdict: The gap between the noise around this and the actual writing is the widest of any recent hit. Kim Soo Hyun and Kim Ji Won are excellent and the opening premise, a marriage that is already dead, is genuinely sharp for four episodes. Then it becomes a terminal illness plot, a chaebol succession war, a stalker thriller, an amnesia arc and an in-law comedy, and it does none of them properly. Sixteen episodes at ninety minutes is a lot of hours for a show that keeps restarting. Watch the first four, then decide honestly whether you want twelve more.

title: Racket Boys
hookNote: Episode 2, once the village and the badminton team are both set up.
endingText: Nobody wins everything. The kids grow, the village holds, and the last episode is a warm goodbye.
verdict: The best show about friendship Korea has made in the Reply era, hidden inside a badminton drama nobody expected. The village is the real subject: parents rebuilding after failure, kids growing up without noticing, and a sport that exists to give them a reason to be in the same room. Sixteen episodes, no villain, no crisis, and a final competition that matters because the people in it matter. The pacing is loose and the romance is barely a subplot, which is exactly right.

title: Reborn Rich
hookNote: Episode 1. He dies and wakes up in 1987 inside the family that had him killed.
endingText: The revenge lands, then the final episode reframes the entire premise and cheapens most of what came before it.
verdict: A transmigration revenge drama where a murdered secretary wakes up inside the chaebol family that killed him, and for fifteen episodes the premise is addictive: Song Joong Ki plays the corporate chess game with visible pleasure and the 1987-forward timeline makes every business move feel consequential. Then episode sixteen happens. The ending reframes the entire premise and cheapens most of what came before it, and it is the single most discussed disappointment of 2022. Watch it for fifteen great hours and brace for the sixteenth.

title: Reborn Rookie
hookNote: Episode 2, once the chairman is stuck in a footballer's body and has to work his way up his own company. The ratings climb through the middle and stay there.
endingText: Tidy and predictable: the swap is undone and the succession settled, with one antagonist given a sadder exit than the setup promised.
verdict: A body-swap business comedy where a chairman wakes up in a footballer's body and has to climb his own company from the bottom. Park Ji Hoon plays the fish-out-of-water with enough charm to carry twelve episodes, and the corporate intrigue is fun if predictable. The ending is tidy, one antagonist gets a sadder exit than the setup promised, and the show never pretends to be anything more than entertaining. Perfectly fine.

title: Reply 1988
hookNote: Episode 3. The first two are scene-setting and the neighbourhood has not clicked yet.
endingText: The husband question is answered plainly. The genuinely sad note is about the alley itself emptying, not about any couple.
verdict: Twenty episodes at ninety five minutes each, and it still goes down in a week. The husband mystery is the worst thing in it, strung out for suspense long past the point it matters, and the show is not really about that anyway. It is about one street, five families, and parents written better than their children, which almost nothing else on Korean television bothers to attempt. Give it four episodes to stop feeling like nostalgia bait, then clear your calendar, because the last two hours play as a bereavement.

title: Reply 1997
hookNote: Episode 1. It moves fast and the fangirl comedy lands immediately.
endingText: The couple reveal is settled early and the finale is a straightforward celebration.
verdict: The first Reply, the cheapest looking one, and the funniest. A Busan fangirl in 1997 organising her whole life around H.O.T was comedy nobody else was making, and the show understands teenage obsession without condescending to it. The husband guessing game is a gimmick, but it is played fairly and settled early, which the later Replies never manage. Sixteen episodes instead of thirty, a flat production and a clumsy reunion frame are the price. If Reply 1988 plays as a bereavement, this one is a party, and it is the right place to start the series.

title: Resident Playbook
hookNote: Episode 3. The first two hours are busy introducing four residents; from three the ward starts running and it does not stop.
endingText: It closes a year of residency with just enough threads left loose for a second season, and none of them feel like a cheat.
verdict: The Hospital Playlist spinoff that had no business being this good. Four first year residents in obstetrics, no band, no cameos leaning on the original, and a deliberately unglamorous specialty where the emergencies are ordinary and constant. Go Youn Jung is excellent and the other three get real arcs rather than support duty. The medicine is accurate enough that people who work in operating theatres say so, and the tone is the Hospital Playlist tone: warm, funny, occasionally devastating, never cruel. Highest comfort score in the 2025 catalog. Start it even if you never watched the parent show.

title: Revenant
hookNote: Episode 5, when the possession stops being a monster of the week and starts being the story of one family's debt.
endingText: The spirit is dealt with and the cost is paid by the living. The final scene is quiet and not consoling.
verdict: Kim Eun Hee wrote it, Kim Tae Ri carries it, and it is Korean folk horror played completely straight: no romance, no comic relief, just five cursed objects and a poor family's inheritance. Kim Tae Ri switching between two people inside one body is the performance of the year. The world building is thin where it needed to be exact, and the middle four hours repeat a shape you have already understood, which is why story lands at 7.2 despite the pedigree. Watch it for the atmosphere and the acting, not the mythology.

title: Revenge of Others
hookNote: Episode 1. The ruling she refuses to accept opens the show.
endingText: The truth about her brother comes out and the people responsible are exposed. The cost is not shared evenly.
verdict: A high school revenge thriller that asks interesting questions about bullying and vigilante justice and then answers them with a plot that cannot keep its own secrets straight. Lomon and Shin Ye Eun are better than the material, the early episodes build genuine tension, and the mystery unravels faster than the show can replace it. Twelve episodes, and the back half coasts on twists that contradict the front half. A good premise wasted by a screenplay that did not plan its own ending.

title: Romance Is a Bonus Book
hookNote: Episode 2, once she is inside the publishing house under false pretences.
endingText: Career and couple both resolve warmly. No third-act betrayal, no manufactured separation.
verdict: The most comfortable watch here and the least ambitious. A divorced copywriter lies her way into an entry level job at the publishing house run by her childhood friend, and the appeal is entirely the office: manuscripts, cover meetings, books treated as a business. Lee Na Young and Lee Jong Suk are warm rather than electric, and the age gap the plot keeps flagging never becomes a real problem. It flattens badly after episode ten, once the story runs out of anything to want. Put it on when you need a drama that will not hurt you.

title: Romantic Doctor, Teacher Kim
hookNote: Episode 1. The operating theatre and the ethics are both live inside the first hour.
endingText: The hospital survives its threat and the last stretch is warm, with a clear door left open for more.
verdict: The best medical drama Korea has made and it is not close. Han Seok Kyu plays a surgeon who chose a country hospital over a career, and the show is about competence as a moral position rather than about who is dating whom. The per-episode ratings sit at or above nine for essentially the whole twenty-episode run, which almost nothing here manages. The hospital politics get repetitive and the romance is the least interesting thing in it, and neither costs it much.

title: Run On
hookNote: Episode 3, once all four leads stop explaining themselves and start talking.
endingText: No grand crisis and no villain. Four adults end up in better jobs and better relationships, having said what they meant.
verdict: A romance about four adults who talk to each other like adults, and the talking is the whole show. Im Si Wan and Shin Se Kyung have a chemistry built on dialogue rather than skinship, and the second couple, played by Kang Tae Oh and Sooyoung, is at least as good. There is no villain, no crisis, and no grand gesture. Sixteen episodes of people saying what they mean is either exactly what you want or the slowest thing you have ever watched. An 8.1 from over sixty thousand ratings, which undersells it: the people who love it, love it completely.

title: Save Me
hookNote: Episode 2, once the family is inside and the door closes behind them.
endingText: The rescue lands and the damage is not undone, so the last hour is relief rather than triumph.
verdict: A grieving family absorbed by a cult, and the frightening part is how reasonable every step of it looks. Seo Yea Ji is excellent as a young woman who understands exactly what has happened to her and cannot get out, and the show refuses to make the cult stupid, which is what makes it work. Four young men trying to reach her is a thin spine for sixteen hours and the middle repeats itself. Heavy, well made, and not remotely a comfort watch.

title: See You at Work Tomorrow!
hookNote: Episode 5, when the first love actually returns rather than being hinted at. Episode 8 is the worst hour in the run by two full points.
endingText: Happy and unearned. The workplace politics that drove the middle are waved away in the final hour.
verdict: An office romcom that hooks at episode five when the first love returns and then craters at episode eight, which is the worst hour in the run by two full points. The workplace politics drive the middle but are waved away in the final hour, and the happy ending feels unearned. A 7.8 that accurately reflects a show with a promising setup and no follow-through.

title: See You in My 19th Life
hookNote: Episode 1, which is the best hour of the twelve. The premise is fully loaded before the first credits roll.
endingText: The central relationship resolves warmly. Two threads the show spent hours building get tidied away in a rush.
verdict: A woman who remembers a thousand years of past lives goes looking for the boy from her last one, and for five hours it is one of the loveliest things tvN aired that year. Shin Hae Sun is superb and the reincarnation rules are handled with a light touch. Then the twelve episode format bites: the per-episode ratings fall from 9.0 to 8.2 without a single upward step, the sister subplot is abandoned, and the finale explains the wrong things. Watch the first half knowing the second half will not honour it.
aliases: Please Take Care of Me in This Life as Well

title: Serendipity's Embrace
hookNote: Episode 1. The reunion happens inside twenty minutes and the eight hours are all aftermath.
endingText: The first love question gets a direct answer and both of them behave like adults about it.
verdict: Eight episodes of a first-love reunion romance that knows exactly what it is and does not waste a minute pretending otherwise. Kim So Hyun and Chae Jong Hyeop have the chemistry the runtime needs, and the show is fluffy, nostalgic, and sweet without ever being interesting. It will not surprise you, challenge you, or stay with you, and it is not trying to. A comfort watch for a slow weekend, no more and no less.

title: Signal
hookNote: Episode 1. The walkie-talkie premise is set up and paid off inside the first hour.
endingText: The central case resolves. The emotional thread does not fully close, and the final minutes are an open door rather than an answer.
verdict: The best plotted procedural in Korean television, and the one to hand to anyone who thinks Korean drama is all romance. A walkie-talkie connects a profiler to a detective in the past, cold cases get solved across twenty years, and the time travel rules are actually enforced, which almost never happens. The cases are grim and specific, and Kim Hye Soo's detective is the heart of it. It ends on a thread that was never resolved on screen, so go in knowing that. No comic relief, almost no romance, no filler.

title: Siren's Kiss
hookNote: Episode 1. The insurance fraud and the attraction are both live immediately, and Park Min Young plays the ambiguity straight from the first scene.
endingText: The reveal satisfies and then the show sprints. Several questions are left standing, and not all of them look deliberate.
verdict: An insurance-fraud thriller with Park Min Young playing the ambiguity straight from the first scene, and for a few episodes the mystery is genuinely compelling. Then the show sprints to the finish, leaves several questions standing, and the reveal satisfies the plot without satisfying the sixteen hours of tension the show built. A 7.7 that reflects a show which started a conversation it could not end.

title: SKY Castle
hookNote: Episode 2, once the coordinator arrives and the rules of the estate are clear.
endingText: The system it spent twenty hours exposing survives, but the families inside it are given a door out.
verdict: A satire about four families in a gated estate destroying their children to get them into medical school, and it is the most watchable ugly show here. The admissions coordinator at the centre is one of the great Korean drama villains, the mothers are written as people rather than types, and the ratings climb from 7.9 to the mid nines and stay there. It is heavy going in the middle, because this is a show about child abuse dressed as class comedy. The last two episodes soften more than the nineteen before them earned.

title: Something in the Rain
hookNote: Episode 1. The two of them are already loaded before either one admits it.
endingText: It reunites them on an ellipsis rather than an argument, and skips the conversation the whole show was building toward.
verdict: Ahn Pan Seok shooting a romance like a European film, all long silences, coffee cups and a camera that will not cut away. The first nine episodes are the best adult romance in this catalog: two people who cannot say what they want, a workplace that punishes women, and a mother who is genuinely frightening. Then it collapses, running the last four hours on repetition and one manufactured obstacle, and the per-episode ratings fall from 9.5 to 7.4 across the run, the steepest drop here. Extraordinary for nine hours, then a slog.
aliases: Pretty Noona Who Buys Me Food

title: Spooky in Love
hookNote: Episode 5, once the case work and the ghosts finally share one plot. Episodes 10 and 11 are where the whole thing comes apart.
endingText: A happy ending visible from a long way off, reached by clearing a checklist of dropped plots in the final two hours.
verdict: Park Eun Bin sees ghosts, a prosecutor sees only evidence, and the twelve episodes promise an investigative occult romance that the show delivers as a generic romcom instead. The comedy is fine, the ghost cases are undercooked, and episodes ten and eleven are where the seams come apart. A happy ending visible from a long way off, reached by clearing a checklist of dropped plots in the final two hours. A 8.1 that reflects goodwill toward the lead rather than satisfaction with the show.

title: Spring Fever
hookNote: Episode 5. The per-episode ratings jump a full point here and stay up: the village stops being scenery and the leads stop bickering.
endingText: Low key and warm, and precisely the ending the genre files under expected.
verdict: A small-town teacher romcom that starts slow, hooks at episode five when the village becomes real, and stays warm through the back half. It is slight and deliberate about being slight, and the per-episode ratings jump a full point once the leads stop bickering. Polarising: half the room sees a cozy gem, the other half sees a show where nothing happens. Both are correct.

title: Squid Game
hookNote: Episode 1. The first game arrives before the hour is out, and the show never needs another pitch.
endingText: The game resolves and the money question gets an answer, at a cost the show makes you feel. The last ten minutes refuse a clean exit and point straight at a sequel.
verdict: The one everybody has seen, and the only one of the three that works from end to end. The games are simple enough to explain in a sentence and cruel enough to hold nine hours, and the debt satire underneath them is blunt but real. Lee Jung Jae plays a weak man rather than a hero, which is what stops the middle turning into a body count. It is not comfort viewing and the writing gets sloppy whenever it leaves the island. Start here, and know that seasons two and three are one story cut in half.

title: Squid Game Season 2
hookNote: Episode 3, when the games restart. The first two hours are recruitment and setup with almost no forward motion.
endingText: It does not end. The season stops in the middle of an arc with nothing settled, because it was shot as one piece with season three.
verdict: Seven episodes that function as a first act, not a season. The new players are thinner than the 2021 cast, the voting mechanic swaps suspense for debate, and the hero spends most of the runtime explaining things the show has already shown. Lee Byung Hun is the best thing in it by a distance. Worth starting only if you are going straight into season three, because on its own this is half a story with no payoff.

title: Squid Game Season 3
hookNote: Episode 1. It picks up mid-collapse, and the second hour is the strongest of the six.
endingText: It closes the story and closes it hard. The final episode chooses bleakness over payoff, and the last scene reaches outside Korea in a way that plays as franchise business rather than an ending.
verdict: The finale the 2021 season did not need. Six episodes, one genuinely great game, and a conclusion that mistakes cruelty for meaning. The baby subplot asks for an emotional investment the writing has not earned, and the Front Man arc resolves on a shrug. Lee Jung Jae is still committed and the production is still immaculate, which makes the hollowness worse rather than better. Watch it to finish what you started, not because it is good.

title: Stranger
hookNote: Episode 2, once the first autopsy contradicts the official story.
endingText: The case closes properly. The institution does not change, and the show is honest that it never will.
verdict: The smartest script on the site and the coldest. A prosecutor who cannot feel much of anything works a corruption case with a detective who feels everything, and the show trusts you to follow a genuinely complicated conspiracy with no recaps. Nobody falls in love and nobody makes a speech: the tension is all institutional politics and who owes whom. It is dense enough that half an episode of inattention will cost you, and the payoff is worth the concentration. Start it awake.

title: Strangers from Hell
hookNote: Episode 2, once the other tenants start knocking on his door.
endingText: The house wins. What the lead has become by the end is the actual horror, not what happens to him.
verdict: Ten episodes of a cheap Seoul boarding house turning an ordinary young man into something else, and the best Korean horror on this list. The threat is not a monster, it is proximity: shared bathrooms, thin walls, neighbours who will not stop knocking. Im Si Wan carries it and Lee Dong Wook's dentist is the most unsettling thing he has played. The first two hours are slow, the violence in the back half is not decorative, and the ending refuses to let the lead out clean. Do not watch it while living alone in a small room.

title: Strong Girl Bong-soon
hookNote: Episode 2, once she is inside the company and the strength has to stay hidden.
endingText: Every threat clears, the couple lands, and the last stretch is almost entirely comic epilogue.
verdict: An 8.7 aggregate, 315,000 watchers, and written reviews that average barely above five out of ten: nothing else in this catalog splits that far. Park Bo Young is the entire reason it works, playing superhuman strength as physical comedy rather than power fantasy, and the office scenes with Park Hyung Sik are genuinely funny. The kidnapping plot underneath is limp, the villain is a cartoon, and the love triangle eats hours it never earns. Come for the lead and the gags and treat every thriller beat as an interruption.

title: Summer Strike
hookNote: Episode 3, once the village regulars start turning up at the library.
endingText: A small mystery closes and she chooses the slower life deliberately. Quiet by design, not by accident.
verdict: A woman quits her job and moves to a seaside village to do nothing, and the show commits to the nothing with more courage than most dramas commit to their plots. Seol In Ah is good in the lead, the village ensemble is warm, and the pacing is deliberately glacial: this is a show about choosing to stop, and it refuses to hurry. The romance is gentle and undramatic, the conflict is mostly internal, and the twelve episodes ask for a kind of patience that is either meditative or unbearable depending on where you are in your own life.

title: Suspicious Partner
hookNote: Episode 1. The wrongful accusation and the meet-cute happen in the same hour.
endingText: The case closes properly and the couple gets a long, warm epilogue.
verdict: A romcom and a serial-killer thriller sharing one show, and the seam is visible in every episode. Ji Chang Wook and Nam Ji Hyun are charming enough that the romance would have carried sixteen hours alone, which makes the murder plot feel like homework whenever it takes over. The per-episode ratings barely move across forty half-hours, which tells you how even it is: never bad, never urgent. Watch it for the leads and let the case wash over you.

title: Tale of the Nine-Tailed
hookNote: Episode 2, once the two brothers share a scene. Their rivalry is the engine.
endingText: A sacrifice lands, then the show finds a route back. Cleaner and cheaper than the same move in Goblin.
verdict: A gumiho fantasy where the two brothers are more interesting than the romance, and the show knows it. Lee Dong Wook and Kim Bum have a rivalry that carries the sixteen episodes better than the love story, which is pretty but predictable. The action is good, the mythology is overstuffed, and the ending makes a sacrifice and then reverses it in a way that is cleaner than Goblin's version of the same move. An 8.4 from 74,000 ratings, and the number is fair: entertaining, occasionally great, never quite as good as the pieces suggest it should be.

title: Tale of the Nine-Tailed 1938
hookNote: Episode 5. The first four hours are a period tour of Gyeongseong; episode 5 is where the trio at the centre starts working and the villain gets a plan worth watching.
endingText: It finishes its own story, then spends its last minutes setting up a sequel that has not arrived. Nothing in season one is contradicted.
verdict: The romance is gone and the show is better for it. This one hands the screen to Lee Yeon, his brother and a third fox, and what comes out is a comic buddy adventure in 1930s Gyeongseong with sharper villains and a tighter plot than the original managed. It is also much lighter: season one could hurt you, and this one is having a good time. You can start here, because the two stories barely touch, which makes it the right entry point if the season one romance was the part you disliked. Just know the last ten minutes are a trailer for a season that never came.

title: Tastefully Yours
hookNote: Episode 3, and the warning goes with it: the run peaks at episode 4 and then drops three full points in two hours.
endingText: Rushed and sugary, with a late twist the ten hours in front of it never asked for.
verdict: A fine-dining romcom that peaks at episode four and then free-falls. The food is gorgeous, the chef-versus-CEO setup is promising, and the lead chemistry is present but underused. A late twist arrives that the ten hours in front of it never asked for, and the ending is rushed and sugary. A 7.8 that reflects a show with beautiful ingredients and no recipe.

title: Taxi Driver
hookNote: Episode 1. The format is fully established inside the first case.
endingText: Case-of-the-week revenge, resolved each time. The season closes with the crew intact and a sequel implied.
verdict: Case-of-the-week vigilante justice with Lee Je Hoon in the driver's seat, and the format works because the real-life cases it draws from generate anger the show can spend. The action is good, the disguises are ridiculous in the best way, and the crew dynamic is warmer than a revenge show has any right to be. It struggles to set a consistent tone, swinging between genuine fury and slapstick inside the same episode, and the overarching plot is the weakest thread. Season one closes cleanly. Start it for the anger, stay for the crew.

title: Taxi Driver Season 2
hookNote: Episode 1. The case format is running inside ten minutes, and the season-long conspiracy can be safely ignored until it turns up.
endingText: Every case closes, the crew ends the season intact, and the door is left open for a third.
verdict: The revenge format still works and the show has stopped pretending to be dangerous. Season one was grimy in a way this one never attempts: the cases are broader, the antagonist is barely on screen, and Kim Do Gi plays closer to a superhero than to a wrecked man doing something illegal. What replaces the grit is the crew, and the Rainbow Deluxe garage is genuinely good company for sixteen hours. That trade makes it a better weeknight watch and a worse drama. Take it as episodic comfort food with a body count, not as the sequel to the thing that unsettled you.

title: Taxi Driver Season 3
hookNote: Episode 1, as always with this show. The first four hours are the best of the season and the cases get thinner after the midpoint.
endingText: The last case closes and the crew gets a lighter, warmer goodbye than forty eight episodes of revenge had earned.
verdict: The third and final season of the most reliable revenge series on Korean television, and reliable is now the problem. The format has not changed in four years: a victim the system failed, a disguise, a beating, a smile. Lee Je Hoon is still excellent and the first four episodes are as good as season two, then the cases start repeating shapes you have already watched twice. If you have seen both earlier seasons you will finish this one out of loyalty and enjoy roughly half of it. If you have not, start at season one, because this ending only means anything with the mileage behind it.

title: Teach You a Lesson
hookNote: Episode 1. The format is set inside the first hour: a school, a crime, a very direct correction. It does not deepen after that, it repeats.
endingText: Episodic to the last hour, so the finale closes the biggest case rather than the system that produced it. Nothing structural is fixed and the show knows it.
verdict: Taxi Driver with a school timetable, and the satisfaction is real: bullies who own their schools get met by a government unit with no interest in process. Kim Moo Yul carries the violence and Lee Sung Min gives the premise more weight than it deserves. The problem is what it does before the correction arrives, because the opening minutes of most episodes are graphic bullying filmed for maximum discomfort, and the show wants that discomfort to be the reason you cheer. Ten episodes of the same beat, a romance subplot nobody needed, and a politics that gets simpler every hour. Watch it for catharsis, not for an argument.

title: The 8 Show
hookNote: Episode 2, once the time for money rule is understood and the floors start turning on each other.
endingText: The show inside the show ends and the eight walk out changed, with no justice handed to anybody.
verdict: The best built satire of the Korean death game wave and the least fun to sit through, which is deliberate. Eight people, eight floors, money that accrues by the second, and a slow slide into cruelty that never needs a masked guard to explain it. Ryu Jun Yeol narrates it like a man describing his own autopsy. The middle is punishing and the last two hours lose their nerve. If Squid Game felt too neat, this is the answer to it.

title: The Apartment Job
hookNote: Episode 1, which opens at 9.4 and holds for four hours. The dip comes later, around episodes 7 and 12.
endingText: It lands. The villains lose, the hero goes legitimate, and a time jump ties the bow neatly.
verdict: A former gangster runs for apartment association president to steal money and accidentally becomes the neighbourhood hero, and the twelve episodes sustain the comedy better than the thriller. The first four hours open strong, the community ensemble is warm, and the villain loses cleanly. A crowd-pleaser that lands its ending, which puts it ahead of most shows in its weight class.

title: The Art of Sarah
hookNote: Episode 4, where the fake identity starts to come apart. The first three hours circle the same reveal without committing to it.
endingText: It closes on an open note with several answers left unspoken, and the resolution it does give is convenient rather than earned.
verdict: A con-artist thriller where the acting is better than the script, and the gap is visible. The fake identity premise is strong, the first four episodes circle the same reveal without committing, and the eight-hour runtime is both the show's strength and its excuse for rushing the ending. The resolution is convenient rather than earned, and several answers are left unspoken on purpose. Worth it for the lead performance, not for the plot.

title: The Atypical Family
hookNote: Episode 7. The con at the centre stops being a con, and both the show and its episode ratings step up and stay up.
endingText: The family gets its powers and each other back, and the central relationship closes cleanly.
verdict: A family of superpowers wrecked by depression, insomnia and phone addiction, which is a far better idea than the marketing suggested. It takes six hours to work out what it is, and once it does the back half is the most emotionally precise fantasy romance of 2024. Jang Ki Yong is quietly devastating as a man who can only travel back to moments when he was happy, and Chun Woo Hee gets the harder role and wins it. The early pacing is a real problem. Push through episode four.
aliases: Although I Am Not a Hero

title: The Auditors
hookNote: Episode 1. The audit team is introduced through a case and the format is clear immediately.
endingText: The corruption case closes and the mentor relationship lands better than the plot does.
verdict: A workplace procedural about corporate auditors that is more entertaining than anyone expected and exactly as long as it needs to be. Shin Ha Kyun plays the mentor as a man who trusts numbers over people, and the rookie's arc is the emotional thread that holds the twelve episodes together. The corruption cases are satisfying in a case-closed way, the romance is minimal, and the finale sticks the landing. An unassuming show that delivers on every modest promise it makes.

title: The East Palace
hookNote: Episode 1. Crown princes start dying before anyone is introduced, which is the most efficient opening of the year.
endingText: The supernatural threat is closed out and the palace politics are not. The final hour spends its time on spectacle rather than on answers.
verdict: Joseon horror with a spirit realm that is openly the Upside Down in hanbok, and for four episodes that is a great trade. The premise is wicked, the production is expensive, and the gore is real: this is a royal bloodbath, not a ghost story with atmosphere. Two problems. The horror stops being frightening once the VFX explains itself, and Nam Joo Hyuk is billed as the lead while the plot belongs almost entirely to Roh Yoon Seo, which is fine as a choice and dishonest as marketing. Eight episodes, strong first half, thin second. Worth it if you want spectacle rather than a mystery that closes.

title: The Fiery Priest
hookNote: Episode 2, once the priest, the prosecutor and the detective are stuck in the same room.
endingText: Every corrupt figure gets a comeuppance staged for maximum crowd noise. Pure catharsis, no melancholy.
verdict: Forty half hours of a short-tempered priest, a cowardly detective and an ambitious prosecutor taking apart a corrupt district, and the funniest action comedy Korea has made. Kim Nam Gil plays rage as slapstick and Lee Ha Nee steals every scene she is handed. It sags around episodes six and seven while the plot sets its pieces, and it never pretends to be about anything deeper than watching bad people lose. For a forty part show the conspiracy is remarkably tidy. Nothing here is rewatched more, and it leaves no hangover.

title: The Frog
hookNote: Episode 3, if you are still there. The two timelines finally start speaking to each other.
endingText: Both timelines conclude and the show declines to explain the woman at the centre of them.
verdict: Two summers, two men, one guesthouse, and eight hours of dread with almost nothing underneath. Kim Yoon Seok and Yoon Kye Sang are excellent and Go Min Si is genuinely frightening, which makes the emptiness of the writing more annoying rather than less. The structure promises a pattern it never delivers, so the ending lands as a shrug instead of a shock. Watch it for the performances. Expect no answers.
aliases: In the Woods With No One
In the Forest With No One

title: The Glory
hookNote: Episode 2, once the board is set and you can see the shape of her plan.
endingText: The plan works. It is cold and complete, and the closing note is nearer to peace than to joy.
verdict: Revenge as a slow administrative process, and that is exactly the appeal. Song Hye Kyo plays a woman who spent eighteen years building a plan instead of healing, and the show never once suggests she should have chosen differently. The school flashbacks are hard to sit through and the plan itself is patient, methodical and satisfying to watch execute. The weakness is the men: the doctor helping her is a device rather than a person, and the second half slows down to admire its own chessboard. Released in two halves, best watched as one piece.

title: The Good Bad Mother
hookNote: Episode 2, once he wakes up changed and the pig farm becomes the whole world.
endingText: It earns its tears instead of buying them. One loss is unavoidable and the show sits in it rather than cutting away.
verdict: A mother-son drama about a woman who raised her child cruelly because the world was crueller, and a prosecutor who has to become a child again, literally, to forgive her. Ra Mi Ran is extraordinary: she plays the damage and the love as the same thing and the show never asks you to decide which is which. The pig farm village is a warm counterweight to the courtroom thriller underneath, and episode two is where it hooks you. It earns its tears honestly, and the ending sits in its loss rather than cutting away from it.

title: The Haunted Palace
hookNote: Episode 3, once the spirit and the palace politics are properly entangled. Sixteen episodes is four more than the story has.
endingText: It resolves the possession and the court plot warmly, several episodes after the ending became obvious.
verdict: A sageuk fantasy where a government official is possessed by a mythical creature and the show plays it for comedy, romance, and palace politics in roughly equal measure. The bromance between the king and the possessed officer is the actual draw, the romance is serviceable, and sixteen episodes is four more than the story needs. The possession premise wears thin in the middle, and the ending is obvious long before it arrives.

title: The Impossible Heir
hookNote: Episode 1. Two boys agree to take over a conglomerate together, and the first four hours are the good ones.
endingText: The partnership ends the only way it can, and the corporate plot stops rather than resolves.
verdict: Four excellent episodes followed by eight that fall apart in real time. The setup is strong: an illegitimate heir, a brilliant friend, and a bargain that cannot survive success. Then the plotting starts inventing conveniences, the female lead is written as a device, and the last stretch is men announcing plans at each other in board rooms. Lee Jae Wook and Lee Jun Young deserved better and clearly knew it. Watch the first four, read a summary, save six hours.

title: The Judge from Hell
hookNote: Episode 1. A demon takes over a judge and starts executing murderers, and the format is set inside one hour.
endingText: The demon's contract resolves and the human cost is settled kindly, with the door left open.
verdict: Park Shin Hye's best performance, in a show that keeps interrupting her to service a romance nobody needed. As a case of the week revenge fantasy it is tremendous fun: the punishments are creative, the two assistants are great, and the swing between comedy and cruelty mostly works. The detective is a flat character played flatly, and every scene that pushes the two of them together drains the tension out of the hour. Watch it for her, and treat the flirting as an ad break.

title: The Judge Returns
hookNote: Episode 1. A corrupt judge dies and comes back with time to spend, and the premise is delivered inside the first hour.
endingText: Ambiguous and rushed. The revenge lands, the moral question the show spent fourteen hours raising does not get an answer.
verdict: A corrupt judge dies and resurrects with a second chance, and the fourteen episodes use the premise for revenge rather than redemption. The action is fun, the corruption mechanics are sharp, and the ending is rushed and ambiguous in a way that feels unfinished rather than deliberate. A premise this good deserved a tighter script and three fewer episodes.

title: The K2
hookNote: Episode 1. The first fight arrives before anything needs explaining.
endingText: The power struggle resolves at real cost, and the personal ending is quieter and sadder than the action promises.
verdict: Ji Chang Wook doing the best action of his career for a show that does not deserve it. The choreography and the stairwell set pieces are excellent, and Song Yoon Ah's political operator is the most interesting person in it by a distance. The romance is the problem: Yoona's character is written as an ornament and the story keeps stopping to protect her. Written reviews rate the story under six out of ten and that is the right call, so come for the action and the villain and expect nothing from the plot.

title: The Legend of Kitchen Soldier
hookNote: Episode 1, which opens at the highest rating of the run. The quest gimmick is explained fast and then gets out of the way.
endingText: It closes the base plot warmly and leaves the door open for a second season rather than finishing the story.
verdict: A military cooking drama with a video-game quest overlay, and the premise is ridiculous enough to be fun. Park Ji Hoon is likeable, the humour works, and the twelve episodes sustain the gimmick better than expected. It closes warmly and leaves the door open for a second season rather than finishing the story, which is either confidence or laziness. A crowd-pleaser that knows exactly what it is.

title: The Legend of the Blue Sea
query: The Legend of the Blue Sea
hookNote: Episode 2, once she is on land and the fish-out-of-water comedy starts.
endingText: The fated-love mechanics pay off and the couple gets a clean landing, after one late scare that goes nowhere.
verdict: Park Ji Eun following her own hit with a mermaid, and it works for exactly as long as Jun Ji Hyun is being funny. The comedy of a sea creature learning Seoul is the best thing in it and the past-life plot bolted alongside is the worst: twenty episodes is four too many and the villain exists to fill them. Lee Min Ho is fine and mostly reactive. Rewatch scores are where it falls apart, because once you know the shape there is very little left to find.

title: The Light in Your Eyes
hookNote: Episode 4. Sit with the confusion, it is doing work.
endingText: A late reframing changes what you thought you were watching. It is devastating and gentle at once.
verdict: Twelve episodes that present themselves as a fantasy romcom about a woman who ages fifty years overnight, then reveal what they were actually doing, and the reveal is the whole drama. Kim Hye Ja is extraordinary, Han Ji Min matches her, and the two of them are playing one person. It is confusing on purpose for four episodes and some of the romance is filler, because the show cannot yet tell you why it is there. The rewatch value is low for an honest reason: once you know, the trick cannot work twice. Worth every minute the first time.

title: The Potato Lab
hookNote: Episode 3. The research station setting and the rivalry both land here, and episode 4 is the best hour before a long slide.
endingText: Warm and slightly hurried, closer to a nice enough after than a full happy ever after, and it leaves two side plots unanswered.
verdict: A mountain-valley romcom set in a potato research centre, and the setting is funnier and more charming than it has any right to be. The rivalry-to-romance arc works, episode four is the high point, and the twelve episodes are pleasant throughout if never urgent. Two side plots are left unanswered and the ending is warm rather than satisfying. A breath of fresh air that does not overstay its welcome.

title: The Price of Confession
hookNote: Episode 1. A woman is arrested for her husband's murder and meets the one person in the prison who wants something from her. The middle sags, the back half is the payoff.
endingText: She gets an ending she has to fight all twelve hours for, and the title is not being metaphorical about what it costs.
verdict: A prison thriller about a woman accused of her husband's murder and the inmate who wants something from her, and the twelve episodes are paced to make you forget you are watching a show with almost no action. The two female leads carry the whole thing, the twists are earned rather than manufactured, and the title is not being metaphorical about the cost. An 8.6 from nearly thirty thousand ratings and one of the tightest thrillers of the year.

title: The Red Sleeve
hookNote: Episode 3, the first time she refuses him and the show reveals what it is actually about.
endingText: History wins. The love is real and complete and still ends the way the historical record says it ends.
verdict: The rare palace romance where the woman's refusal is the plot. A court lady wants to remain her own person, the crown prince wants her, and the drama takes the power gap between them seriously instead of finding it romantic. Lee Junho is very good and the historical detail is unusually careful. It sags in the middle, the court scheming is thin next to the central relationship, and the ending is exactly as sad as history requires it to be. Watch it if you want a sageuk romance that argues with itself.

title: The Tale of Lady Ok
hookNote: Episode 1. A slave takes a dead noblewoman's name and starts practising law with it, and the first three hours are the highest rated of the run.
endingText: A positive ending for a sageuk this dark, reached through a final case that resolves faster than it should.
verdict: A sageuk legal thriller where a slave takes a dead noblewoman's identity and starts practising law, and the first three episodes are the best in the run. The cases are gripping, the lead is magnetic, and the sixteen episodes sustain the tension better than most sageuks manage. The romance works, the politics are dense, and the final case resolves faster than it should. An 8.6 from over twenty thousand ratings, and it is the best historical drama of 2025.

title: The Trauma Code: Heroes on Call
query: The Trauma Code Heroes on Call
hookNote: Episode 1. A surgeon arrives from a war zone and starts breaking hospital policy inside twenty minutes. There is no slow build anywhere in the eight hours.
endingText: The hospital politics close out and the team is left standing, with an unmistakable opening for more.
verdict: Eight episodes, no romance, no filler, one absurdly competent trauma surgeon against a hospital that would rather protect its margins. It is a fantasy and it is completely upfront about being one, which is why it works where earnest medical dramas stall. Ju Ji Hoon is having more fun than he has had in years and the resuscitation sequences are shot like action. The recipe underneath is the Dr. Romantic recipe with the sentiment stripped out, so if you have seen that, you have seen the bones of this. Best binge on this list if you want momentum over depth.
aliases: The Trauma Center: Heroes on Call

title: The Trunk
hookNote: Episode 4, where the trunk plot finally moves. The three hours in front of it are mood with almost no story.
endingText: The mystery gets an answer and the marriage does not really get one. It stops on an image rather than a conclusion.
verdict: Beautifully shot, immaculately scored, almost completely inert. Eight episodes about a company that arranges one year marriages, a premise with obvious teeth the show refuses to bite with. Seo Hyun Jin and Gong Yoo are both good and both stranded in scenes that end before anything gets said. The mystery is thin enough to summarise in one sentence. Watch it for the craft or skip it entirely.

title: The Whirlwind
hookNote: Episode 1. The prime minister makes his move against the president inside twenty minutes.
endingText: The power struggle concludes and the cost is total. Nobody involved keeps what they wanted.
verdict: The most underwatched Korean drama of 2024 and the best political thriller Netflix has in Korean. Twelve episodes of two people who are both right and both monstrous, played by Sul Kyung Gu and Kim Hee Ae at the top of their range. It is dense, it assumes you can follow a cabinet reshuffle, and it never slows down to explain itself. No romance, no comic relief. If Stranger worked for you, this is the one nobody mentioned.

title: The Wonderfools
hookNote: Episode 3. The first two hours are loud and shapeless and the powers are played as a gag; from three onward the trio becomes a unit and the 1999 doomsday setting starts doing real work.
endingText: The crisis closes and the trio is left wide open for more. Not a cliffhanger, not a full stop either.
verdict: A superhero comedy set in the last year of the millennium, which sounds like a tonal disaster and mostly is not, because Yoo In Shik knows how to make absurd things feel lived in. Park Eun Bin and Cha Eun Woo have the best comic chemistry of the year and the millennium dread bleeds into the characters instead of just decorating them. Eight episodes, no filler, the highest rewatch scores in this catalog. It is messy for two hours and the emotional beats in the back half land harder than a comedy needs them to. The one honest warning: the first two episodes are the worst two, so judge it at three.

title: The Worst of Evil
hookNote: Episode 1. The undercover assignment starts immediately and the marriage is already a wound before the first hour ends.
endingText: The operation closes the way the first episode implies it will. What it costs is the whole point of the last hour.
verdict: A country cop goes undercover in a Gangnam drug ring in 1995 while his wife, a detective, works the other side of the same case. This is the best written thing in the 2023 slate: 9.6 across the written reviews with a 9.1 rewatch score, which almost nothing in the catalog matches. Ji Chang Wook has never been better and Wi Ha Joon plays the gang boss as somebody worth loving, which is what makes the ending land. It is also 18 plus, sustained, ugly violence with no relief valve. The spiritual heir to Cruel City, and better paced than it.

title: Thirty but Seventeen
hookNote: Episode 2, once she is in the house and the two histories start touching.
endingText: Everything gets tied off, including the strand about the accident, and the last episodes are pure warmth.
verdict: A woman wakes from a thirteen-year coma still seventeen, in a house owned by a man who has spent those years refusing to feel anything. It is a healing drama that actually does the work, giving both leads a reason to be broken and then repairing them slowly and specifically. Shin Hye Sun is why it holds: playing seventeen at thirty without making it a gimmick is much harder than it looks. Nothing here is surprising, and that is the point rather than a flaw.

title: Thirty-Nine
hookNote: Episode 3, once the diagnosis is out in the open. It stops being a hangout show.
endingText: You know where this is going by the third hour, and it goes there. The friendship is the only consolation offered.
verdict: Three best friends turning forty, one of whom is dying, and the show never pretends that the friendship can fix what is coming. Son Ye Jin leads an ensemble that plays adult grief without melodrama, and the male leads are genuinely supportive rather than decorative. It is not a romance, it is a friendship elegy, and the pacing is slow because the subject demands it. The ending goes where the diagnosis promised it would go, and the only consolation on offer is that the three of them had each other.

title: Through the Darkness
hookNote: Episode 2, once the first interview subject starts talking and the method becomes visible.
endingText: No single case caps it. The unit survives institutional resistance and the work is allowed to continue.
verdict: A criminal profiling drama based on Korea's first real profiler, and the procedural half is better than the personal half. Kim Nam Gil gives the lead the right quiet intensity, and the interview sequences, particularly the early ones, are gripping in a way that pure exposition rarely is. It loses steam as the cases become less specific and the time jumps get confusing, and the supporting cast is underwritten. Worth it for the method rather than the plot: it is one of the few shows that makes the work of understanding a killer feel like real work.
aliases: Those Who Read Hearts of Evil
Those Who Read the Minds of Evil

title: To My Beloved Thief
hookNote: Episode 1. The night thief and the prince collide immediately and the body swap arrives before you have time to get bored of either of them.
endingText: It closes properly, both the swap and the family debt, and it does not cheat to get there.
verdict: A physician by day and a Hong Gil Dong by night, a prince who cannot decide whether to arrest her or help her, and a body swap that for once is not an excuse for a week of comedy. Nam Ji Hyun is the reason it works and Moon Sang Min is the surprise. What lifts it above the KBS weekend sageuk average is discipline: sixteen episodes that actually resolve, humour that never derails the plot, and a second female lead written as a person. The weak spot is the law, which the script applies whenever it wants the leads to suffer and forgets whenever it would solve something. Good comfort sageuk, better than its rating suggests.

title: Tomorrow
hookNote: Episode 2, once the case-of-the-week structure clicks into place.
endingText: Every case is about somebody choosing to stay alive. The finale closes the leads own backstory kindly.
verdict: A fantasy about grim reapers who prevent suicides, and the subject matter is handled with more care and courage than the genre packaging suggests. Each case is about somebody choosing to stay alive, and the show takes each one seriously without being manipulative. Kim Hee Sun and Rowoon lead with contrasting energy that works, and the backstory pays off in the final stretch. The middle sags and the mythology is sometimes in the way of the cases, but the best episodes are genuinely powerful. An 8.8 from over seventy thousand ratings, and the show deserves it for the ambition alone.

title: Touch Your Heart
hookNote: Episode 1. The premise is set up and paid off inside the hour.
endingText: No obstacle survives the last two episodes, and it finishes on a proposal-shaped scene.
verdict: An actress hiding out as a secretary in a law firm, made almost entirely of Lee Dong Wook being stiff and Yoo In Na being warm at him. It is fluff with no engine, which is fine for eight hours and a problem for sixteen: the per-episode ratings fall from the mid eights to under seven across the middle stretch and never fully recover. The legal cases are throwaway and the second-lead threat does not exist. Watch it if you want a low-stakes hangout with two leads you already like.

title: Trigger
hookNote: Episode 3, once the guns are circulating and the premise stops being a lecture about them. Episode 6 is the peak.
endingText: The buildup gets a payoff that arrives far too quickly and asks you to accept a great deal on the way out.
verdict: A gun-control thriller set in a country with almost zero gun crime, and the first three episodes build the premise with genuine tension. Then the logic starts dying before the characters do: the plot holes multiply faster than the body count, and the ending arrives far too quickly for the moral question the show spent ten hours raising. Strong start, weak finish, and the 8.3 is an average of two very different halves.

title: Tunnel
hookNote: Episode 1. A 1986 detective lands in 2017 inside the first twenty minutes.
endingText: The killer is caught, the time-travel logic pays off cleanly, and the family thread resolves warmly.
verdict: A 1986 detective chasing a serial killer falls through a tunnel into 2017, and for seven episodes it is nearly as good as Signal. The premise is used properly: a competent policeman whose methods are thirty years obsolete, played for comedy and then for loss. Then the back half gets careless, the cast start missing what you worked out two episodes earlier, and it should have ended at twelve. The killer is caught, the time logic holds and the family thread lands warmly, which is more than most of these manage. Watch Signal first, then this.

title: Twenty-Five Twenty-One
hookNote: Episode 2, once the two of them start meeting at night. Episode 1 is loud and abrasive on purpose, and it is the easiest place to quit.
endingText: The friendships and the growing up land beautifully. The romance does not end the way fourteen episodes trained you to expect, and the reason it gives is not good enough.
verdict: Fifteen episodes of the best youth writing in years, then a finale that spends the goodwill in one hour. The fencing, the 1998 setting and the friendship between the two girls are exceptional, and the first love material is written with real specificity. The framing device is the problem: it commits early to an outcome, hides from it for fourteen hours, then delivers it badly. Episode sixteen is the steepest single-episode drop in this catalog. Watch it knowing that, and consider stopping at fifteen.

title: Twinkling Watermelon
hookNote: Episode 2, once he lands in 1995 and meets his father at eighteen.
endingText: The timeline is repaired without erasing anybody. The family ends the show intact and much closer.
verdict: A time travel show about a hearing child of deaf parents, and much better than that premise suggests. The boy goes back to 1995 and meets his father as a teenager, and the whole trick is letting him see a person instead of a parent. The band material is charming, sign language is treated as a language rather than as decoration, and the emotional payoffs are set up hours in advance. It is sentimental and it earns all of it. The most underwatched show in this catalog relative to how good it is.

title: Typhoon Family
hookNote: Episode 3. The IMF collapse hits the family firm properly here and the show finds its subject. The last four hours are the weakest.
endingText: The company survives and the family debt closes, with the final hour doing more work than the four before it.
verdict: A family drama set during the 1997 IMF crisis, and the period setting gives the family conflict real economic stakes rather than manufactured ones. The ensemble is strong, the father-son dynamic is the emotional core, and the show finds its subject properly around episode three. Sixteen episodes is too many for the story it is telling, and the last four hours are the weakest. Worth it for the period atmosphere and the performances.

title: Uncle Samsik
hookNote: Episode 4, where the political machinery behind the partnership becomes visible.
endingText: The alliance breaks along the lines it was always going to break along, and history wins.
verdict: A political thriller set in 1960s Korea that asks you to invest in two men whose partnership is doomed by history, and then delivers on the doom. Song Kang Ho grounds the whole thing, and Byun Yo Han matches him, which is the highest compliment available. It is slow, talky, and dense with period politics that demand attention, and the 7.5 rating reflects a show that alienated a romance audience rather than a show that failed. If the subject interests you, it is excellent. If it does not, nothing here will convert you.

title: Undercover High School
hookNote: Episode 1. An intelligence agent enrolls as a student and the show tells you within one hour that logic is optional. The last three episodes are the strongest.
endingText: The operation closes cleanly and the school plot lands exactly where it has been pointing since the first hour.
verdict: An NIS agent goes undercover in a high school, and the pleasure is entirely Seo Kang Joon, who plays an absurd part with total commitment and drags twelve episodes along behind him. Nothing here holds up to a second thought: the plot is a chain of events rather than a story, and the school is whatever the week needs it to be. But it is funny on purpose, the action is decent, and Jin Ki Joo makes the teacher more than a foil. Weekend television that knows what it is. Do not go in wanting the spy thriller the poster implies.

title: Undercover Miss Hong
hookNote: Episode 3, once the disguise stops being the joke and the fraud case starts moving. The setup hour is the weakest thing in sixteen episodes.
endingText: The con pays off and the caper closes properly. The last three hours are tidier and much less funny than the middle.
verdict: A financial regulator goes undercover as a twenty year old temp inside a securities firm during the IMF crisis, and the show is smart enough to build its best running joke out of the fact that Park Shin Hye does not look twenty. What starts as workplace farce turns into a Robin Hood revenge caper somewhere around the middle, and the turn is genuinely well engineered. Sixteen episodes is two too many and the late 1990s setting is getting crowded on Korean television right now. Still the funniest thing on tvN this year and the best Park Shin Hye has been in a decade.

title: Vagabond
hookNote: Episode 1. The crash and the cover-up are both in motion immediately.
endingText: It stops rather than finishes, on a deliberate cliff for a continuation that was never made.
verdict: The most expensive action Korea had shot for television at the time, and for fifteen hours it is a genuinely great conspiracy thriller: a stuntman investigating the plane crash that killed his son, a cover-up reaching the presidential office, set pieces that hold up next to film. Lee Seung Gi is better here than his reputation suggests and Bae Suzy is used properly. Then it does not end. The final hour opens a new problem instead of closing the one you watched sixteen episodes for, and the second season it was setting up never happened.

title: Vigilante
hookNote: Episode 1. The double life is established in the first twenty minutes and the pursuit starts immediately.
endingText: The final hour resolves one hunt and deliberately leaves the larger question open for a second season that may never come.
verdict: A police cadet spends his nights beating the sentences the courts were too soft to hand out. Nam Joo Hyuk is genuinely good as a blank, and Yoo Ji Tae is better as the man who wants to sponsor him. Eight tight 44 minute hours, excellent fight choreography, and a moral argument the script keeps setting up and then dodging: every time it should ask whether he is right, it cuts to another beating. Great to watch, thin to think about, and the ending is a sequel hook rather than an ending.

title: Vincenzo
hookNote: Episode 3, when the Geumga Plaza tenants stop being obstacles and become his crew.
endingText: The villains are dealt with on the show's own gleeful terms and the lead chooses exile over redemption. Plays as satisfying, not sad.
verdict: Twenty episodes of cartoon violence played completely straight, and the tone is the whole test. If a mafia consigliere torturing a corporate lawyer for laughs sounds like a good evening, this is one of the most entertaining shows on the site. If it does not, nothing here improves. It is at least four episodes too long, the plaza tenants turn into a variety act, and the romance is decoration on a revenge machine. Song Joong Ki has never been better cast. It rewatches poorly, which is what happens when the pleasure is all in the surprise.

title: W: Two Worlds
hookNote: Episode 1. She is pulled into the webtoon before the first hour is out.
endingText: The meta rules are used to earn a happy ending rather than to dodge one.
verdict: The best opening four episodes and one of the worst back halves in this catalog. A surgeon is pulled into her father's webtoon, and the drama spends its first hours inventing rules that are genuinely thrilling, then spends its last hours breaking them whenever the plot needs an exit. Lee Jong Suk and Han Hyo Joo are excellent and the villain is one of the best in Korean television. By episode twelve the logic does whatever it likes and the tension goes with it. Watch it for the setup and accept that the happy ending is bought rather than earned.

title: Weak Hero Class 1
hookNote: Episode 1. Eight episodes, zero filler, and the first fight tells you exactly what kind of show this is.
endingText: The violence has consequences that cannot be undone. The last episode takes something away and does not give it back.
verdict: Eight episodes of forty minutes with nothing wasted, the most efficient thing on this site. It looks like a school fight show and it is actually about a boy who is very good at hurting people and very bad at keeping anyone. The violence is ugly rather than cool, which is exactly why the last episode lands the way it does. It is also relentless and offers no relief anywhere.
