Watch it in one sitting, and do not expect season two to do the same job.

title: Weak Hero Class 2
hookNote: Episode 1. The first fight lands immediately, which is also the problem: nothing in this season is allowed to build.
endingText: A cost is paid and acknowledged, and it is not the permanent kind season one dealt in. It closes on an unmistakable setup for a third season.
verdict: Netflix money bought better fights and cost the show its subject. Season one was a tragedy about loneliness that happened to contain violence; this is an action series with eight episodes of forty minutes trying to carry an arc the webtoon spends hundreds of chapters on, so friendships that should be earned simply appear fully formed. The choreography and the budget are a clear step up, and Park Ji Hoon is still the reason to watch. Watch it if the fighting was the draw. Do not start the series here, and do not expect the ending of season one to hit twice.

title: Weightlifting Fairy Kim Bok-joo
hookNote: Episode 2, once the two leads start colliding on purpose.
endingText: Everyone gets what they were training for, more or less. No cruelty anywhere in the last stretch.
verdict: The friendliest romance on this list and the one where nothing bad happens to anyone. Two college athletes become friends and then a couple with no triangle, no misunderstanding held for four episodes and no parent to defeat, which in 2016 was close to radical. Lee Sung Kyoung and Nam Joo Hyuk are the reason it is still recommended. The catch is that the sport evaporates: by the second half nobody is training and the show has no engine left except sweetness, which is where its written reviews turn on it. Watch it for the relationship, not the story.
aliases: A Fada do Levantamento de Peso

title: Welcome to Samdal-ri
hookNote: Episode 8, when the show finally drops the career scandal plot and becomes the hometown drama it was always trying to be.
endingText: Both families make peace with an old death and the childhood couple gets a clean, unambiguous ending.
verdict: Jeju, a disgraced photographer, the weather forecaster who has loved her since childhood, and a village full of people with opinions. The back half is excellent and the per-episode ratings show it, climbing from 8.7 to 9.3 and staying there. Getting to it means sitting through seven hours of a Seoul cancellation plot that the writing has no interest in, which is why a warm show scores 6.8 on story and 4.8 on rewatch. Ji Chang Wook and Shin Hae Sun are worth the patience. Skim the first quarter.

title: What's Wrong with Secretary Kim
hookNote: Episode 1. The dynamic is fully loaded from the first scene.
endingText: A childhood-trauma reveal is handled gently, then it is all epilogue and wedding energy.
verdict: The most watched romcom in this catalog and the thinnest. Park Seo Jun's narcissist and Park Min Young's secretary have chemistry enough to carry sixteen episodes with almost no plot underneath, and for eight of them that is plenty. Then the childhood trauma reveal arrives, amnesia gets treated as a legitimate engine, and everything slows to fill the remaining hours. Written reviews rate it far below its 8.5 aggregate, and that gap is the honest summary: easy to enjoy, hard to defend. Come for the leads and expect nothing from the story.
aliases: Why Would Secretary Kim Do That

title: When Life Gives You Tangerines
hookNote: Episode 2, where the childhood section pays off.
endingText: Time does what time does. The final act asks you to accept a loss and be grateful anyway.
verdict: One of the ten highest rated Korean dramas ever made, and it earns that without doing anything clever. Four seasons, one Jeju family, sixty years, and a script that treats ordinary lives as though they were worth sixteen hours, because they are. IU is very good and Moon So Ri, playing the same woman older, is better. It is engineered to make you cry, you can see the engineering, and it works anyway. The only real caveat is that it never surprises you: this is the best possible version of exactly what it looks like.

title: When the Camellia Blooms
hookNote: Episode 2, once the town starts talking about her and Yong-sik starts visibly not caring.
endingText: The serial-killer thread closes, the town comes round, and the single mother gets an uncomplicated win.
verdict: A single mother running a bar in a town where everyone talks about her, plus a serial killer, plus the most straightforwardly decent man on Korean television, and all three somehow fit. Gong Hyo Jin plays someone who has apologised for existing her whole life and stops doing it, and Kang Ha Neul is the warmest romantic lead here. The mystery is functional rather than clever, and forty parts means several detours that go nowhere. What it gets right is the town: gossip as a weapon, community as the thing that finally protects her. It ends kindly and earns it.

title: When the Phone Rings
hookNote: Episode 1. The kidnapping call happens immediately and the marriage plot is running by minute twenty.
endingText: Everything resolves, including the parts that did not need resolving. The final hour is the weakest of the twelve.
verdict: A contract marriage, a kidnapping, and a thriller that moves faster than any romance drama has a right to. Twelve episodes with no filler, a sign language premise the show actually uses, and Yoo Yeon Seok playing cold better than he plays warm. The plotting gets silly in the back half and the finale hands out happy endings like party favours. Neither costs it much: this is the most propulsive romance thriller since Vincenzo, and it knows exactly how long to stay.

title: While You Were Sleeping
hookNote: Episode 2, once the three of them realise they are dreaming the same futures.
endingText: The premonitions resolve, the antagonist is stopped, and the found family gets a warm coda.
verdict: The most watchable half of a great drama. Three people dreaming each other's futures, a rookie prosecutor trying to prevent crimes he has already seen, and a first half that is structurally clever and beautifully shot. Then it settles into a case-of-the-week legal show with a stalker who reappears whenever an emergency is required, and the final ten half hours are stretched thin. Lee Jong Suk and Bae Suzy are good and the supporting trio around them is better. Watch the first sixteen with confidence and the rest with a lowered bar.

title: Wonderful World
hookNote: Episode 1. The loss, the killing and the prison sentence are all inside the first hour. There is no slow build.
endingText: The larger conspiracy closes and the mother is allowed something like peace. It earns that ending.
verdict: The revenge drama of 2024, and it gets there without a single clever twist. A psychology professor loses her son, the legal system shrugs, she handles it herself in the first hour, and the remaining thirteen deal with what that costs her. Kim Nam Joo is extraordinary and Cha Eun Woo is better here than anywhere else he has worked. Nothing about the plot is new. The performances make it land anyway.

title: Youth of May
hookNote: Episode 2, once the blind-date deception turns into something real.
endingText: It is set in Gwangju in May 1980 and the history is not softened. The framing device tells you early how this goes.
verdict: A romance set in Gwangju in May 1980, and the history is not softened. Lee Do Hyun and Go Min Si play the love story with a tenderness that makes the political violence around them feel personal rather than decorative, and the show earns its tragedy by spending its first half being gentle. The framing device tells you early how this goes, and the final episodes deliver on the promise. An 8.7 from over thirty thousand ratings, and it is one of the best period romances Korea has made.
